1	# Porting techniques
2	
3	Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
4	do, and what it did the last time.
5	
6	## Build-time patch
7	
8	When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
9	1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
10	20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.
11	
12	- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
13	- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
14	  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
15	  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
16	  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
17	  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
18	- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
19	- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
20	  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
21	  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
22	  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
23	  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
24	  fail.
25	
26	## Single precision
27	
28	When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
29	The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.
30	
31	- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
32	  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
33	  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
34	  filled.
35	- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
36	  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
37	  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
38	- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
39	  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
40	  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
41	  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
42	  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
43	  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
44	  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
45	  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
46	  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
47	  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
48	  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
49	- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
50	  and now go through it too, with `single_constants.h` (`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`) and
51	  `single_frand.h`. Run `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` on the
52	  wrapper's object after `pio run -e stopwatch`: any count in a per-frame
53	  function means a literal, macro or `double` struct field the rename missed
54	  (`x11shim.md` has the four that did). A trig argument that is a big whole
55	  number is a fifth: look at a frame before trusting the float build.
56	- A plain single-precision wrapper is cheap to try: include
57	  `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and `<name>_floatlit.c`, exclude
58	  the original in the three `build_src_filter` lines and list the name in
59	  `patch_float_literals.py`. Measure it on the board and drop it if it moves
60	  nothing. On the board, step before to after: Hopalong 7-20 to 3.4 ms,
61	  WhirlWindWarp 6-26 to 3.8 ms, BinaryHorizon 95.8 to 31.8 ms, Barcode 77.1 to
62	  56.1 ms (frames byte-identical), XSpirograph 44.2 to 10.9 ms, Vines 182 to
63	  10.3 ms; Bouboule stayed at 14.5 ms.
64	- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
65	  literals first.
66	- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
67	  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
68	- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
69	  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
70	  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
71	  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
72	- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
73	  12.5 fps.
74	- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
75	  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
76	  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
77	  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
78	  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
79	  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
80	  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
81	- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
82	  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
83	  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
84	- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
85	  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
86	  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
87	  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
88	  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
89	  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
90	  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
91	  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
92	  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.
93	
94	## Slow hack
95	
96	When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
97	(`step` in the serial line is large).
98	
99	- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
100	  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
101	  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
102	  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
103	- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
104	  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
105	  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
106	  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
107	  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
108	- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
109	  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
110	  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
111	  board.
112	- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
113	  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
114	  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
115	  committing.
116	- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
117	  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
118	- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
119	  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
120	  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
121	- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
122	  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
123	  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
124	  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
125	  a ring in two spans a row.
126	- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
127	  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
128	  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
129	  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
130	  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
131	- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
132	  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
133	  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
134	  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
135	  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
136	  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
137	  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
138	  the fit is unchecked.
139	- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
140	  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
141	  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
142	  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
143	  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
144	  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
145	- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
146	  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
147	  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
148	- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
149	  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
150	  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
151	- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
152	  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
153	  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
154	  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
155	  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
156	  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
157	- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
158	  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
159	  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
160	  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
161	  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
162	  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
163	  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
164	  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.
165	- Before writing a speed override, grep the hack's header and glue for the
166	  author's own knob (`GLB_SLOW_GL` in `bubble3d.h`, set from the wrapper with
167	  `#undef` and `#define` after the header). It keeps the copy byte-identical
168	  and is the trade the author intended: Bubble3D went from 4-5 fps to a mean
169	  of 11.4. A hack split over several files (entry point in one, work in
170	  another) gets one `<name>_*gl.c` wrapper per file, and only the file that
171	  does the maths needs `single_precision.h`.
172	
173	## Thin lines in a GL hack
174	
175	When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
176	in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
177	time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.
178	
179	- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
180	  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
181	  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
182	- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
183	  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
184	  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
185	  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
186	- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
187	  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
188	  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
189	  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
190	  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
191	  show any effect.
192	- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
193	  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
194	  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
195	  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
196	  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
197	  it should ask.
198	- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
199	  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
200	  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
201	- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
202	  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
203	  absence of vanishing lines alone.
204	
205	## Stack check
206	
207	When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
208	AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
209	cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
210	first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.
211	
212	Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
213	1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
214	KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
215	frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
216	decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
217	rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
218	replay it from every start.
219	
220	## Large allocations
221	
222	When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.
223	
224	- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
225	  numbers are double the device's.
226	- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
227	  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
228	  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
229	- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
230	  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
231	  for each large hack.
232	
233	## Images
234	
235	Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
236	`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
237	bitmap. There is no PNG
238	decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
239	mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
240	`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
241	image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.
242	
243	A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
244	script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.
245	
246	## Pixmap double buffering
247	
248	When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
249	result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
250	Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
251	buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
252	every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
253	straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
254	when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)
255	
256	- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
257	  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
258	- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
259	  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
260	  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
261	  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
262	  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
263	  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
264	  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
265	- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
266	  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
267	  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.
268	
269	## Restart leak test
270	
271	When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
272	example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
273	before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
274	`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
275	hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.
276	
277	Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
278	0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.
279	
280	On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
281	Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
282	at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.
283	
284	## Stopping before the first draw
285	
286	When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
287	but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
288	press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
289	sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
290	`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
291	frames exited 139.
292	
293	- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
294	  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
295	- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
296	  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
297	  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
298	- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
299	  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
300	- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
301	  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
302	  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
303	  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
304	  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).
305	
306	## Tests that cannot be fooled
307	
308	A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
309	window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
310	deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
311	(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.
312	
313	A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
314	pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
315	passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
316	keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
317	show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
318	background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
319	old start.
320	
321	A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
322	keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
323	63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
324	a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
325	(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
326	and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
327	Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
328	wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.
329	
330	## Wrapping an xlockmore hack's init or draw
331	
332	Emptying `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` (Blaster) fails: the hack includes
333	`xlockmore.h`, which has no include guard and defines it again. Rename the
334	hack's tables instead (`#define pipes_xscreensaver_function_table
335	pipes_upstream_xscreensaver_table`, the same for `_xlockmore_function_table`),
336	include the hack, `#undef` both, define the wrappers, then
337	`#define draw_pipes pipes_draw_no_fade` and call
338	`XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2("Pipes", pipes, pipes)`. See `hacks/pipes_gl.c`.
339	
340	## Background colour
341	
342	The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
343	as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
344	on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.
345	
346	## Skipping a hack
347	
348	Threads and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and the
349	reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
350	abandoned. Xft text used to be on this list; it is not now (see "Xft text").
351	
352	## Xft text
353	
354	A hack that draws with Xft (`XftDrawStringUtf8`, `load_xft_font_retry`) needs
355	the stand-in in `x11shim/xft.h`. Its font is Special Elite, rasterised at build
356	time into pixel-coverage tables (`firmware/font_atlas.py`, which runs
357	`tools/make_font_atlas.py` on the TTF in `firmware/assets/fonts/`), and
358	`main.cpp` installs it with `xshim_set_font`. Only ASCII has glyphs: anything
359	else draws as `?`. The family in a font name is ignored and the baked size
360	nearest the number is used, so to change a hack's text size override its font
361	resource (XJack's `XJACK_FONT_PX`) and bake the size in `font_atlas.py`.
362	
363	Our `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, because that would change what
364	every hack sees. Build the hack through a wrapper that includes it first
365	(`hacks/xjack_xft.c`), and exclude the original from all three
366	`build_src_filter` lines. XJack's wrapper shows two things an Xft hack may
367	need from `screenhack.c`: the window background set from the `background`
368	resource (`XClearWindow` otherwise clears to black), and a reshape after
369	init. Tests that run the hack install `test_font.h`'s blocky font, so a
370	pinned hash does not follow FreeType; with no font installed the shim gives a
371	blank one, so a test that replays every hack does not abort.
372	
373	## Worktree setup
374	
375	A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
376	symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
377	named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
378	with every worktree: ask Rod first.
379	
380	A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
381	computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
382	`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.
383	
384	## Device capture
385	
386	- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
387	  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
388	- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
389	  data verified".
390	- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
391	  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
392	- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
393	  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
394	- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
395	  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
396	  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
397	  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
398	- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
399	  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
400	  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).
401

# Porting techniques

Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
do, and what it did the last time.

## Build-time patch

When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.

- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
  fail.

## Single precision

When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.

- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
  filled.
- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
  and now go through it too, with `single_constants.h` (`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`) and
  `single_frand.h`. Run `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` on the
  wrapper's object after `pio run -e stopwatch`: any count in a per-frame
  function means a literal, macro or `double` struct field the rename missed
  (`x11shim.md` has the four that did). A trig argument that is a big whole
  number is a fifth: look at a frame before trusting the float build.
- A plain single-precision wrapper is cheap to try: include
  `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and `<name>_floatlit.c`, exclude
  the original in the three `build_src_filter` lines and list the name in
  `patch_float_literals.py`. Measure it on the board and drop it if it moves
  nothing. On the board, step before to after: Hopalong 7-20 to 3.4 ms,
  WhirlWindWarp 6-26 to 3.8 ms, BinaryHorizon 95.8 to 31.8 ms, Barcode 77.1 to
  56.1 ms (frames byte-identical), XSpirograph 44.2 to 10.9 ms, Vines 182 to
  10.3 ms; Bouboule stayed at 14.5 ms.
- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
  literals first.
- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
  12.5 fps.
- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.

## Slow hack

When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
(`step` in the serial line is large).

- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
  board.
- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
  committing.
- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
  a ring in two spans a row.
- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
  the fit is unchecked.
- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.
- Before writing a speed override, grep the hack's header and glue for the
  author's own knob (`GLB_SLOW_GL` in `bubble3d.h`, set from the wrapper with
  `#undef` and `#define` after the header). It keeps the copy byte-identical
  and is the trade the author intended: Bubble3D went from 4-5 fps to a mean
  of 11.4. A hack split over several files (entry point in one, work in
  another) gets one `<name>_*gl.c` wrapper per file, and only the file that
  does the maths needs `single_precision.h`.

## Thin lines in a GL hack

When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.

- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
  show any effect.
- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
  it should ask.
- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
  absence of vanishing lines alone.

## Stack check

When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.

Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
replay it from every start.

## Large allocations

When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
  numbers are double the device's.
- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
  for each large hack.

## Images

Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
bitmap. There is no PNG
decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.

A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.

## Pixmap double buffering

When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)

- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.

## Restart leak test

When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.

Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.

On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.

## Stopping before the first draw

When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
frames exited 139.

- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).

## Tests that cannot be fooled

A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.

A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
old start.

A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.

## Wrapping an xlockmore hack's init or draw

Emptying `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` (Blaster) fails: the hack includes
`xlockmore.h`, which has no include guard and defines it again. Rename the
hack's tables instead (`#define pipes_xscreensaver_function_table
pipes_upstream_xscreensaver_table`, the same for `_xlockmore_function_table`),
include the hack, `#undef` both, define the wrappers, then
`#define draw_pipes pipes_draw_no_fade` and call
`XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2("Pipes", pipes, pipes)`. See `hacks/pipes_gl.c`.

## Background colour

The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.

## Skipping a hack

Threads and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and the
reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
abandoned. Xft text used to be on this list; it is not now (see "Xft text").

## Xft text

A hack that draws with Xft (`XftDrawStringUtf8`, `load_xft_font_retry`) needs
the stand-in in `x11shim/xft.h`. Its font is Special Elite, rasterised at build
time into pixel-coverage tables (`firmware/font_atlas.py`, which runs
`tools/make_font_atlas.py` on the TTF in `firmware/assets/fonts/`), and
`main.cpp` installs it with `xshim_set_font`. Only ASCII has glyphs: anything
else draws as `?`. The family in a font name is ignored and the baked size
nearest the number is used, so to change a hack's text size override its font
resource (XJack's `XJACK_FONT_PX`) and bake the size in `font_atlas.py`.

Our `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, because that would change what
every hack sees. Build the hack through a wrapper that includes it first
(`hacks/xjack_xft.c`), and exclude the original from all three
`build_src_filter` lines. XJack's wrapper shows two things an Xft hack may
need from `screenhack.c`: the window background set from the `background`
resource (`XClearWindow` otherwise clears to black), and a reshape after
init. Tests that run the hack install `test_font.h`'s blocky font, so a
pinned hash does not follow FreeType; with no font installed the shim gives a
blank one, so a test that replays every hack does not abort.

## Worktree setup

A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
with every worktree: ask Rod first.

A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.

## Device capture

- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
  data verified".
- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail. Add `test_<name>_stops_do_not_leak` beside the others, and
   mutation-check it: remove each free a wrapper adds and watch it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again. A new hack never gets
   `0` in `kBaseline`: `0` is for a hack left unpinned on purpose, with the
   reason in its comment (DecayScreen, RotZoomer).
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
   and came back through issue #37): remove it
   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
   to.
   Unhook its build steps too: its entry in `patch_float_literals.py` and any
   pre-script only it needs (BlockTube's `gl_textures.py`), or every build
   still runs them and fails without their `vendor/` input.
9. A header that a pre-script writes into the build dir (the font, the grab
   image) must be included under `__has_include` in `native/dump_main.c`:
   `tools/probe_hacks.py` compiles that file without the build's generated
   directory, and an unconditional include failed two `test_probe_hacks`
   cases. Add the pre-script to all three `extra_scripts` lines in
   `platformio.ini`, and a wrapper's original source to all three
   `build_src_filter` lines (`sed -i.bak 's|<last entry>$|<last entry> <new>|'`
   does all three).

22	# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas
23	
24	OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
25	`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.
26	
27	- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
28	  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
29	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
30	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
31	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
32	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
33	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
34	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
35	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
36	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
37	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
38	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
39	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
40	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
41	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
42	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
43	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
44	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
45	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
46	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
47	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
48	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
49	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
50	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
51	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
52	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
53	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
54	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
55	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
56	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
57	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
58	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
59	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
60	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
61	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
62	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
63	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
64	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
65	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
66	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
67	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
68	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
69	  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
70	  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
71	  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
72	  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
73	  new hack for both.
74	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
75	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
76	  neither.
77	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
78	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
79	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
80	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
81	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
82	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
83	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
84	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
85	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
86	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
87	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
88	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
89	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
90	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
91	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
92	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
93	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
94	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
95	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
96	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
97	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
98	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
99	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
100	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
101	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
102	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
103	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
104	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
105	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
106	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
107	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
108	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
109	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
110	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
111	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
112	  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
113	- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
114	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
115	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
116	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
117	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
118	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
119	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
120	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
121	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
122	  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
123	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
124	  to reach them.
125	- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
126	  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
127	  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
128	  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
129	  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
130	  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
131	  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
132	  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
133	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
134	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
135	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
136	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
137	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
138	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
139	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
140	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
141	  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
142	- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
143	  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
144	  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
145	  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
146	  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
147	  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
148	- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
149	  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
150	  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
151	  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
152	  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
153	  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
154	- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
155	  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
156	  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
157	  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
158	  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
159	- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
160	  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
161	  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
162	  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
163	  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
164	  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
165	  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
166	  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
167	  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
168	  drift from the firmware's rule.
169	- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
170	  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
171	  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
172	  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
173	  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
174	  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
175	  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
176	  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
177	  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
178	  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
179	  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
180	  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
181	  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
182	- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
183	  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
184	- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
185	  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
186	  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
187	  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
188	- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
189	  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
190	  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
191	  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
192	  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
193	  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
194	  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
195	- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
196	  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
197	  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
198	  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
199	  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
200	  the clears that ran, for the tests.
201	- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
202	  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
203	  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
204	  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
205	- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part
206	  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
207	  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
208	  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
209	  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
210	  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
211	  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
212	- The push overlap (`repaints_all`, issue #118): before each clear or
213	  primitive, `follow_canvas` points TinyGL's `pbuf` at the current
214	  `canvas->px`. The colour dirty rectangle is kept per buffer (the buffer
215	  just left keeps its box, valid flag and clear colour), so a clear still
216	  rewrites only what was drawn in that buffer; a buffer TinyGL never drew in
217	  gets a full clear. The box last drawn in the buffer just left is marked
218	  erased, since that is what the display shows. The swap does not follow:
219	  a frame that draws nothing must mark nothing, or the push would send the
220	  older frame the new buffer holds. If the two buffers' clear colours
221	  differ, the switch marks the whole canvas: the clear finds its own buffer
222	  already that colour and rewrites nothing (red, green, red left the
223	  display green). `glshim_canvas_overwritten()` forces a full clear for
224	  writers other than TinyGL (`test_push_overlap`'s noise
225	  run). Not for a scale-2 hack (`double_into_canvas` writes only the box) or
226	  Pipes (skips clears). Pinned A/B, plain to overlapped: Bubble3D 11.2 to
227	  12.0 fps, Gears 15.2 to 16.5, CubicGrid 15.3 to 19.5, StonerView 36.4 to
228	  43.8, HexTrail 15.2 to 20.5 before its first restart; Morph3D about 3%
229	  (small push), unflagged. The step grew 5 to 10 ms with both cores on
230	  PSRAM.
231	- The swap marks two bounding boxes (erased, drawn), not a list of
232	  regions: a drawing in the top half and an erase in the bottom one mark
233	  every row between. A test that asserts a row stays clean must keep both
234	  frames' drawings on one side of it (`corner_frame(f % 2)`).
235	- Board profiles (issue #43): `-DGL_PROFILE` prints a `glprof` line after
236	  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
237	  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
238	  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
239	  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
240	  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
241	  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
242	  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
243	- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores
244	  TinyGL's order): a vertex is lit when something that uses it is drawn, so
245	  culled triangles cost nothing. Gears 61.1 to 57.7 ms, Morph3D 61.4 to
246	  58.4 ms, frame hashes unchanged. `GL_IRAM` (still a switch) and two
247	  experiments since removed, matrix stacks in internal RAM and the data
248	  cache's next-line prefetch (autoload) over PSRAM, moved Gears by under 1 ms.
249	  The prefetch needs a region that holds only mapped pages: over the whole
250	  32 MB data bus it boot-looped the board (the panic handler faulted too), and
251	  a region worked out from an allocation's address cannot promise that.
252	- Fill is compute-bound, not PSRAM-miss-bound. A new PSRAM cache line costs
253	  129 cycles to read and about 220 to read and write back (the `membench`
254	  line of a profile build), but neighbouring triangles reuse lines. A banded
255	  renderer that held a frame's triangles and replayed them into 32-row bands
256	  in internal RAM was exact but slower: Gears 59 to 76 ms (replay 38 ms
257	  against 30 ms of direct fill), Hypnowheel 476 to 528 ms. It was reverted
258	  (`feature/43-banded-renderer` history). Faster fill needs fewer cycles a
259	  pixel or fewer pixels, not other memory.
260	- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
261	  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
262	  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.
263	- Resolving a merge conflict in `tools/tinygl_patch.py`: the conflict region
264	  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,
265	  so keeping both sides can put an entry in the wrong tuple (a `Replace` among
266	  the `Hot` entries fails collection with "'Replace' object has no attribute
267	  'definition'"). Check each kept entry's tuple. `ruff format` on the file also
268	  rewraps an `AA_LINE +` line nobody touched; revert that hunk.
269	- `glshim_set_render_scale(2)`, read by the next `glshim_open`, renders at half
270	  the width and height: `glViewport` is a macro for `glshim_Viewport`, which
271	  divides by the scale, and the swap doubles the dirty box into the canvas.
272	  Hypnowheel's fill went from 334 to 129 ms (not a quarter: rows and triangles
273	  still cost). Nothing registered uses it.
274	- Added for the 2026-10-12 batch, each test-first: `glInterleavedArrays` for
275	  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);
276	  `glTexImage2D` converting RGBA and luminance bytes to RGB (TinyGL exits on
277	  anything but three-component `GL_RGB`); `glColor4ub`; `glTexGeni`,
278	  `glDepthFunc` and `glTexEnvf` accepted and ignored; `glTexParameterf`; the
279	  OpenGL 1.2 colour-control names; and `texfont.h` (`texfont.c`), which draws
280	  TinyGL's public-domain 8x8 font as quads at half the point size.
281	- TinyGL fills a quad over [10, 16] by [23, 24] as columns 9 to 15 and both
282	  rows: its edges are inclusive, so test text and thin quads by their box,
283	  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.
284	- TinyGL prints a warning for every `glEnable` it does not know, each time,
285	  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the
286	  wrapper.
287	- Pipes (issue #44, `hacks/pipes_gl.c`) skips work no other GL hack can: with
288	  its camera fixed (`*rotatepipes: False`), when the clear, both matrices and
289	  the lists called so far match last frame, it skips the clear and those lists
290	  and draws only the new piece. Two traps, each caught by
291	  `test_pipes_incremental_redraw_matches_a_full_redraw`: a new screen
292	  recompiles the same list names, so any `glNewList` must end the skipping; and
293	  the next screen must be generated at the start of a draw, as upstream's fade
294	  does, because `generate_system` clears, and a clear after the swap erased the
295	  frame just shown in a full redraw. `pipes_full_redraw` turns the skipping off
296	  for the tests.
297	- Pipes compiles every display list of a screen when the screen starts, and a
298	  list holds each vertex expanded (a 16 by 16 sphere from `glDrawArrays` is
299	  about 17 KB). Board PSRAM sets the screen size (`-DPIPES_CYCLES`,
300	  `-DPIPES_SIZE`), and TinyGL does not check a list's allocation, so running
301	  out crashes: 3 systems of 150 left 1.9 MB free. Host heap for the same lists
302	  is about twice the board's (8-byte list words).
303	- Pipes' helpers: `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` (a triangle table,
304	  `teapot2.h`, instead of evaluators TinyGL lacks). That table was 228 KB of
305	  flash; since #104 `firmware/teapot_table.py` writes `generated/teapot/`, a
306	  byte-identical copy of `teapot.c` beside a `teapot2.h` holding the floats
307	  deflated (37 KB), so the copy's quoted include finds ours first.
308	  `glshim/glx_teapot.c` renames upstream's `unit_teapot` and unpacks the table
309	  into 227 KB of PSRAM only while it runs (Pipes calls it once, compiling a
310	  list); with no memory the teapot is an empty list. `test_glshim` compares
311	  the unpacked floats with upstream's. `buildlwo.c` maps `GL_POLYGON` to
312	  `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` in its own wrapper only (issue #80 is the general
313	  question).

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1

  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.

  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own

  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
