  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.

  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.

  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.

  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.

  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed

  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a

  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables

  the clears that ran, for the tests.

  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.

  (see `hacks.md`). The budget model predicted 106 ms a frame with scanlines
  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,
  but the model reads one early frame and the hack's cost grows over its
  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).

  primitive, `follow_canvas` points TinyGL's `pbuf` at the current
  `canvas->px`. The colour dirty rectangle is kept per buffer (the buffer
  just left keeps its box, valid flag and clear colour), so a clear still
  rewrites only what was drawn in that buffer; a buffer TinyGL never drew in
  gets a full clear. The box last drawn in the buffer just left is marked
  erased, since that is what the display shows. The swap does not follow:
  a frame that draws nothing must mark nothing, or the push would send the
  older frame the new buffer holds. If the two buffers' clear colours
  differ, the switch marks the whole canvas: the clear finds its own buffer
  already that colour and rewrites nothing (red, green, red left the
  display green). `glshim_canvas_overwritten()` forces a full clear for
  writers other than TinyGL (`test_push_overlap`'s noise
  run). Not for a scale-2 hack (`double_into_canvas` writes only the box) or

  regions: a drawing in the top half and an erase in the bottom one mark
  every row between. A test that asserts a row stays clean must keep both
  frames' drawings on one side of it (`corner_frame(f % 2)`).

  each `run` line with cycle counts per stage (clear, list, vertex, shade,
  tri, fill, point, line; nested, so vertex includes tri and fill), and
  `tools/ab_flash.py` builds variants pinned, flashes them in turn and
  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:
  PlatformIO cleans a build directory, image and all, when the build flags
  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.

  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.

  not a pixel count. Its lit textures can lose a step of a channel.

  which on the board goes to the serial log every frame: filter them in the

  the unpacked floats with upstream's. `buildlwo.c` maps `GL_POLYGON` to

472	  profile put 220 of a 300-390 ms step in a software-double `cos` per nudge
473	  axis per vertex: `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` is single precision (frames
474	  byte-identical). Upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` (set in `bubble3d_gl.c`) takes
475	  the sphere from 1,280 to 320 triangles: 4-5 fps became mean 11.5, worst
476	  window 8.2, with the push (12-24 ms, a full frame) now a fifth of the frame.
477	  It is flagged `repaints_all` since the GL layer follows the canvas swap
478	  (issue #118): 11.2 to 12.0 fps, worst window 8.0 to 8.8. Upstream's
479	  default `transparent` skips the depth test and expects a blend TinyGL's fill
480	  does not do, so back faces overwrote front faces as a dark wedge in each
481	  bubble (found by the trail review): the registry overrides `*transparent:
482	  False`, which enables the depth test. It cost nothing measurable on the
483	  board (mean 11.5 before, 11.4 after).
484	- Bubbles (`bubbles_safe.c`, `bubbles_sprites.py`) is three copied files and
485	  44 PNGs (four sets of eleven sizes: blood, blue, glass, jade) that the
486	  pre-script deflates into the build dir with `make_logo_blob.py --deflate`,
487	  never committed. Upstream's free leaks every live bubble in the mesh lists
488	  and one extra step pixmap: the wrapper frees both, and the leak test fails
489	  if either free is removed (checked by mutation). `bubbles.h` includes
490	  `<X11/Xlib.h>`, which the shim now answers with a header that pulls in
491	  `xshim.h`. A host dump always shows the same set, so seed `random()` to see
492	  the others (jade, blue and glass came up in six seeds, blood did not).
493	  Blood is teal with red mottling in the source art, not red: Rod saw cyan
494	  with red spots on the panel and it matches `blood11.png`, so it is not a
495	  byte swap. A single frame can show a bubble with a bite out of it while
496	  neighbours merge and are redrawn; the bite is gone a few frames later. On
497	  the board it ran at 54-62 fps (mean 57.4), a 5-7 ms step under its own
498	  9.5 ms wait, and held nothing in PSRAM: it is paced by its delay, not by the
499	  work.

---
paths:
  - "firmware/src/hacks/**"
  - "firmware/patch_*.py"
  - "firmware/pacman_sprites.py"
  - "tools/maze_patch.py"
  - "tools/pacman_patch.py"
---

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps (14 with 64-byte cache lines); overlapping the push with
  the next step (`repaints_all`) takes it to 19 fps. Other ideas are in issue
  #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass the
  objects still showed soft-double helpers: Interaggregate's were `frand` in
  `build_field` (fixed with `single_frand.h`); Halftone's, Anemone's and
  Euler2D's are in `*_init` only, once a start. `tools/softdouble_report.py`
  lists them by function.
- To see which hacks are worth a look, flash a build with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=20`,
  log the serial port for one lap (about 40 minutes), and run
  `uv run tools/triage_hacks.py lap.log --soft` (after `pio run -e stopwatch`).
  It sorts each hack into step-bound, push-bound or paced (its own delay is the
  biggest part of the frame) and puts the soft-double calls in its object
  beside it. A hack that is step-bound with calls is a wrapper candidate;
  step-bound with none is in its drawing, not its maths (Braid, Marbling,
  Discrete, BinaryRing); paced ones gain only what the step saves, down to the
  delay (Forest 500 ms, Vines 200 ms). A wrapper that moves nothing is worth
  dropping: Bouboule built single stayed at 14.5 ms, because its cost is
  ellipse fills.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moved between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grew and shrank, so its
  fps was 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window said. Upstream opens every frame
  by filling the whole window black, which is a full frame of PSRAM writes
  (229,000 pixels a frame on the host, the strokes only about 16,000 of them),
  so `anemone_direct.c` erases only where last frame's lines were
  (`span_erase.h`, each line's box grown by its round caps): 31,000 pixels, the
  same frames, and only those rows dirty. On the board, over one 20 s window
  per lap: 30.5 fps mean (worst 20.4), step 25.2 ms. Counting pixels and
  spans written a frame on the host (a temporary counter in `hspan`) is a
  quick way to see what a hack costs before the device does. Forest waits
  500 ms between trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls
  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. Cheaper: drop a temporary
  `src/hacks/zz_seed_tmp.c` with that constructor, guarded by `SEED` being set
  (`-e dump` builds every file under `src/`), run
  `SEED=n .pio/build/dump/program <index> <frames> out.raw`, and delete the
  file before running the tests. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
  random state differs by then.
- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  registers through `xmatrix_direct.c` with `*trace: False`, which skips the
  typed "connecting" sequence it would open with (the rare "Knock, knock,
  Neo" event, `knockKnock`, is still on); `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0
  out.raw` names the allocating line in seconds (rebuild `-e dump` first: a
  `pio test` deletes the program).
- Starfish and Goop spent most of a frame in the shim's polygon fill (double
  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon
  in float, optionally mixed in at an alpha in 32nds (all three colour
  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is integer now
  (see `x11shim.md`; Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.
- Loop asks for 100 ms between generations (8.7 fps with a 3.5-7 ms step); the
  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md.in`).
  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.
- A full-frame write to the PSRAM canvas costs about 25 ms whatever does it
  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.
- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`
  (67 to 42 ms) and frees each circle's high fringe, which upstream's free
  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).
- BinaryRing (`binaryring_single.c`) is told the display is 24 bits deep: its
  16-bit path drops every hit below one 5-bit step, so only green builds up
  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:
  the 32-bit image was put a pixel at a time, 130 of a 240 ms step.
  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.
- GraphStat's word list (`graphstat.h`) is copied from `vendor/` at build
  time (`firmware/vendor_data.py`); since 6.17 upstream ships the header, each
  word wrapped in `_()` for `gettext` (`x11shim/include/nls.h`). Its timing
  is in frames tuned for 30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s
  instead of 12.
- EtruscanVenus (`etruscanvenus_single_gl.c`) runs on a 48 by 32 grid
  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;
  `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU`, `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV` and `-DETRUSCANVENUS_FULL`
  try others. Its modes differ: those that fill the screen are fill-bound.
  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).
- BlockTube was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and not much going on);
  its source, notices row, `blocktube_single_gl.c`, `gl_textures.py` and
  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring
  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and
  `blocktube` (with its `count_the_blocks`) to `patch_float_literals.py`
  again. It drew 400 blocks
  (`tools/blocktube_patch.py`, upstream's 1,000) at half resolution with a
  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters
  `glEnable` of fog and texture generation, which TinyGL warns about every
  frame.
- Companion Cube and Floppy are not ported (Rod dropped both, listed in
  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).
- Rocks and DecayScreen were wired, looked at and dropped in the 2026-10-12
  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it
  runs at 17.2 fps against its own 50 ms delay, and holds 2.66 MB of PSRAM and
  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
  all looked at).
- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.
- XJack (`xjack_xft.c`) types "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" in
  Special Elite on cream paper, through the Xft stand-in. Its first host frames
  were black (it clears the window, and the shim cleared to black) and then
  half-drawn lines scrolled in from the bottom (`xjack_init` sizes the page
  before its 40 pixel margins, and xscreensaver reshapes it after): the wrapper
  sets the window background and calls `xjack_reshape`, and each has a test
  that fails without it. Upstream's `font2` of 12 is small on a 466 pixel
  panel: Rod found 16 small and 20 good, so the wrapper overrides it to 20
  (`-DXJACK_FONT_PX=<12|16|20|24>`; about 28 columns). The margins swing
  (modes 1 to 4 walk them diagonally on purpose), and the round bezel cuts the
  corners of the page. Rod has seen it on the panel. It runs at 8-16 fps, set
  by its own delay (`wait` is 46-130 ms): typing is a 0.1 ms step, scrolling
  3.9-13.8 ms with pushes of 74-241 rows. It holds no PSRAM, and a 6-minute
  capture lost 352 bytes of internal heap in three steps (see
  `assessment_measured.md.in`).
- The 2026-10-13 sixth batch (Marbling, Deco, IMSMap, MetaBalls, Munch, CCurve,
  BinaryHorizon, RotZoomer, Twang, NerveRot, Flow, Bouboule, Ant, HyperBall,
  Demon, Droste, Polyominoes, Barcode) passed every host test and then four
  of them failed on the board, none of which a host frame could show: a stack
  overflow (Polyominoes), an allocation too big for PSRAM that the host's lazy
  memory allowed (Flow), 0.6 fps (Marbling) and 1.6 fps (Droste). Flash a
  batch before calling it done. A rotation build starting at the first new
  hack (`-DSTART_HACK=\"marbling\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=30`) measures all of them
  in one 10 minute capture. Rod then took MetaBalls, Twang, Flow and Droste
  out of `g_hacks[]` (slow or margin-bound, not worth tuning). Their sources,
  wrappers and wrapper tests stay in the tree, unregistered; to bring one
  back, re-add its registry entry, expected name, pin and leak test.
- Marbling does a 5-iteration fractal noise per pixel (12 ms a step on the
  host, 1,785 ms on the board, so the host suite takes about 3 minutes
  longer). `marbling_safe.c` overrides `*gridsize` to 6 and `*iterations` to 3
  (5.4 fps, cells of 6 pixels). Upstream's `marbling_free` never frees its
  colour table (5 KB a start): the wrapper does.
- Polyominoes (`polyominoes_iterative.c`, `tools/polyominoes_patch.py`) panicked
  the board with a double exception inside `count_adjacent_blanks`: a flood
  fill that calls itself once for each blank cell, up to 360 deep in several
  puzzles, 32 bytes a level on top of the solver's frames. The build now
  replaces it with a loop over an explicit stack (frames identical to the
  recursive build). Read a puzzle hack's grid sizes, not just its frame size.
- Flow's `csegs` is `(count + 36) * ncolors * taillen` segments of 8 bytes:
  upstream's 3,000 bees and 200 colours is up to 29 MB, which the host
  provided lazily and the board refused, so the hack drew one frame and
  nothing more. The registry gives it 120 bees and 8 colours. In single
  precision its flow dies out within about 600 frames (the screen stays
  black), so it is double: 3.0-4.8 fps, about 200 ms of every step being its
  search for the next flow. A single frame at 300 frames looked right in
  both: sweep several frame counts (300, 1000, 3000) for a hack that
  restarts itself or can die out.
- CCurve's `*limit` of 200,000 segments (each a malloc and a recursion) took
  740 ms in single precision and 2.9 s in double; the wrapper caps it at 30,000.
  Its 1.4 fps is its own pacing: 0.4 s between iterations, 42 ms of work.
- Droste (`droste_small.c`) hands back a loader token on the first call and
  finishes on the next, with the pixmap's size as the rectangle, so upstream's
  own "just finished" branch runs. It loads a picture the size of the window,
  not 2.5 times it (5.4 MB as the 32-bit image `XGetImage` makes), and renders
  at half width and height through `lowrez_put.h` (630 ms became 190 ms, 4.6
  fps). `XPutPixel` is mapped to swap the pixel, since `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565 and the picture holds canvas order. MetaBalls takes all but
  28 KB of the internal heap while it runs (466 row buffers of 466 bytes).
- RotZoomer and Twang (`rotzoomer_single.c`, `twang_single.c`) start their
  picture and tiles the first time `draw` finds `load_image_async_simple`
  finished. The shim finishes at once and returns NULL, so that branch never
  ran and the first draw used a NULL zoom box (exit 139). Each wrapper does
  the finishing step straight after init. Changing the shim to return a loader
  would also change Boxfit and DecayScreen, so it is Rod's call. Both are
  single precision (they call `sin` and `cos` in double for every pixel).
  RotZoomer is unpinned in `test_hacks.c`: with no grab image every frame is
  black.
- BinaryHorizon (`binaryhorizon_swapped.c`) is told the display is 24 bits
  deep. Its 16-bit path adds less than a step of a channel per hit and rounds
  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it
  restarts and callocs a new pixel buffer without freeing the old one (868 KB
  on the device): the wrapper frees it and clears the window.
- Munch defaults to `*xor: True`, so `XDrawPoint` honours `GXxor` now (only
  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own
  `i_log2` and `to_pow2`. IMSMap needed 1-bit `XYBitmap` images, `BitmapPad`
  is 32, and Deco needed `allocate_writable_colors` and `XStoreColors` (no
  writable cells). The scorer's gap lists were wrong twice: MetaBalls'
  `XListPixmapFormats` is under `#if 0`, and Ant needed only `automata.h`, a
  file in `hacks/` that is now copied to `xs_support/`.
- NerveRot passes the address of its own `double` locals to `rgb_to_hsv`, so
  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test
  under AddressSanitizer found it as a stack-buffer-overflow, but a host frame
  looked right.
- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,
  drawn with `GXor`, which the shim does not do. The registry overrides
  `*use3d: False` (a single colour cycling through the palette) and
  `*cycles: 0`. Twang's 3 by 3 tiles of 120 pixels leave black margins and
  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.
- A wrapper that finishes an image load itself (RotZoomer, Twang, Droste) must
  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.
- A wrapper that clears state before upstream's own timed check (BinaryHorizon
  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
  clock whose second read is later.
- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only
  through start and stop.
- Deluxe's `draw_star` (ten sin/cos in software `double`, #54 idea 5): a
  single-precision build gave identical frames and no device gain (step
  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the
  mask and the strokes.
- Bubble3D is four files (`b_lockglue.c` holds `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, so the
  scorer knows it as `b_lockglue`; `SOURCE_STEMS` in `score_hacks.py` maps the
  registry name `bubble3d` to it), each built as its own `USE_GL` unit by
  `bubble3d_*gl.c`. Only `bubble3d.c` has a licence text; Rod chose to list the
  other four under its notice. The glue's `init()` builds a sphere and drops it
  (leaked on every start: the wrapper makes that call return NULL). A GL
  profile put 220 of a 300-390 ms step in a software-double `cos` per nudge
  axis per vertex: `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` is single precision (frames
  byte-identical). Upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` (set in `bubble3d_gl.c`) takes
  the sphere from 1,280 to 320 triangles: 4-5 fps became mean 11.5, worst
  window 8.2, with the push (12-24 ms, a full frame) now a fifth of the frame.
  It is flagged `repaints_all` since the GL layer follows the canvas swap
  (issue #118): 11.2 to 12.0 fps, worst window 8.0 to 8.8. Upstream's
  default `transparent` skips the depth test and expects a blend TinyGL's fill
  does not do, so back faces overwrote front faces as a dark wedge in each
  bubble (found by the trail review): the registry overrides `*transparent:
  False`, which enables the depth test. It cost nothing measurable on the
  board (mean 11.5 before, 11.4 after).
- Bubbles (`bubbles_safe.c`, `bubbles_sprites.py`) is three copied files and
  44 PNGs (four sets of eleven sizes: blood, blue, glass, jade) that the
  pre-script deflates into the build dir with `make_logo_blob.py --deflate`,
  never committed. Upstream's free leaks every live bubble in the mesh lists
  and one extra step pixmap: the wrapper frees both, and the leak test fails
  if either free is removed (checked by mutation). `bubbles.h` includes
  `<X11/Xlib.h>`, which the shim now answers with a header that pulls in
  `xshim.h`. A host dump always shows the same set, so seed `random()` to see
  the others (jade, blue and glass came up in six seeds, blood did not).
  Blood is teal with red mottling in the source art, not red: Rod saw cyan
  with red spots on the panel and it matches `blood11.png`, so it is not a
  byte swap. A single frame can show a bubble with a bite out of it while
  neighbours merge and are redrawn; the bite is gone a few frames later. On
  the board it ran at 54-62 fps (mean 57.4), a 5-7 ms step under its own
  9.5 ms wait, and held nothing in PSRAM: it is paced by its delay, not by the
  work.

1	# Porting techniques
2	
3	Recipes for the traps listed in `SKILL.md`. Each says when it applies, what to
4	do, and what it did the last time.
5	
6	## Build-time patch
7	
8	When: the hack's own constants make it too big for the board. Maze keeps a
9	1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one `calloc`, about
10	20 MB, and the board has 8 MB of PSRAM.
11	
12	- The copy in `hacks/<name>/` stays byte-identical to upstream (`cmp` it).
13	- A PlatformIO `pre:` script (`firmware/patch_maze.py`) writes a patched copy
14	  into the build directory, using a tested function (`tools/maze_patch.py`)
15	  that raises if upstream's lines change. A wrapper (`hacks/maze_small.c`)
16	  includes that copy, and the original is excluded in `build_src_filter` of
17	  all three environments (`stopwatch`, `native`, `dump`).
18	- Maze's limits went from 1000 to 80: about 125 KB.
19	- A patch can switch off a branch (Pacman's `NRAND (2) == 0` becomes `0`) or
20	  replace a whole function (its route search becomes a loop). Check the
21	  original's SHA-256 so an upstream edit fails the build. Before a rewrite, pin
22	  a long-run fingerprint taken with the original (30,000 frames, every ghost's
23	  position every 100), show the code ran, and mutate the order to watch the pin
24	  fail.
25	
26	## Single precision
27	
28	When: a hot loop does `double` maths or calls `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt` or `pow`.
29	The ESP32-S3 has a single-precision FPU only, so double runs in software.
30	
31	- Find the hot loop first and count the calls. Substrate makes four `sin` calls
32	  per sand grain, with 64 grains a crack and up to 100 cracks: about 25,000
33	  software `sin`s a frame. Its step grew from 5 ms to 121 ms as the picture
34	  filled.
35	- Wrapper `hacks/<name>_single.c`: include the framework headers first, then
36	  `hacks/single_precision.h`, then the unmodified hack. Exclude the original in
37	  `build_src_filter` of all three environments.
38	- `M_PI` is a double literal, so the angle arithmetic stays double: put
39	  `#undef M_PI` and a float definition after the header. Literals such as
40	  `0.81` stay double too, and a header cannot change them: `0.5 * x` with a
41	  float `x` is software double maths. Check the wrapper's object for soft-double
42	  helpers with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm braid.o | grep ' U __.*df'` (compile with
43	  `-Os -mlongcalls` and the shim's include paths). If any remain, rewrite the
44	  literals at build time as Braid does: `tools/float_literals.py` (tested, skips
45	  strings and comments) run by `firmware/patch_float_literals.py`, and the
46	  wrapper includes `<name>_floatlit.c` from the build directory. GCC's
47	  `-fsingle-precision-constant` does the same, but Apple clang ignores it, so
48	  host tests would run other arithmetic than the board.
49	- Galaxy, Drift, Discrete, Flame and Substrate were wrapped before this check
50	  and now go through it too, with `single_constants.h` (`MAXRAND`, `M_PI`) and
51	  `single_frand.h`. Run `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` on the
52	  wrapper's object after `pio run -e stopwatch`: any count in a per-frame
53	  function means a literal, macro or `double` struct field the rename missed
54	  (`x11shim.md` has the four that did). A trig argument that is a big whole
55	  number is a fifth: look at a frame before trusting the float build.
56	- A plain single-precision wrapper is cheap to try: include
57	  `single_precision.h`, `single_constants.h` and `<name>_floatlit.c`, exclude
58	  the original in the three `build_src_filter` lines and list the name in
59	  `patch_float_literals.py`. Measure it on the board and drop it if it moves
60	  nothing. On the board, step before to after: Hopalong 7-20 to 3.4 ms,
61	  WhirlWindWarp 6-26 to 3.8 ms, BinaryHorizon 95.8 to 31.8 ms, Barcode 77.1 to
62	  56.1 ms (frames byte-identical), XSpirograph 44.2 to 10.9 ms, Vines 182 to
63	  10.3 ms; Bouboule stayed at 14.5 ms.
64	- Hand-written `sin` and `cos` (`hacks/fast_trig.h`) moved Braid by 5%. Do the
65	  literals first.
66	- Compare double and float frames at several counts. Early frames match; a
67	  chaotic hack diverges later but should keep its look.
68	- GL hacks too: Hypnowheel's spiral called `cos` and `sin` in `double` for
69	  every vertex, about 275 ms of a 706 ms step, hidden behind a fill-heavy look.
70	  Its wrapper (`hypnowheel_single_gl.c`) adapts `get_position` and
71	  `get_rotation` as HexTrail's does.
72	- Results: Galaxy 5 to 14 fps. Substrate step 119-121 ms to 37-38 ms, 6.2 to
73	  12.5 fps.
74	- A hack that passes the address of its own `double` local to a shim function
75	  (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &s, &v)`) writes eight bytes into a four-byte float, and
76	  the compiler does not warn. Moire's frames were all different from the
77	  double build's until `moire_single.c` mapped the call to an adapter defined
78	  before `single_precision.h`. Cmp the wrapper's frames against the unmodified
79	  hack's. A hack with no decimal literals must stay out of
80	  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses it.
81	- Once the maths is float, look at the fills before the next idea. CWaves'
82	  cosines were 4 ms of a 61 ms step; its 233 column fills were 57 (a thin
83	  full-height rectangle touches a new cache line a store). See `hacks.md`.
84	- A float build can break a check that held in double. Both the S3 (`madd.s`)
85	  and arm64 fuse a multiply and an add, so `t*n - floor(t*n)` uses the exact
86	  product for the subtraction and the rounded one for the `floor`, and can
87	  come out slightly negative: Celtic's `assert(tt>=0 && tt<1)` aborted at
88	  t 0.331093 with 3422 segments. The 3000-frame test (`pio test`) found it
89	  on the host, and the same abort would have hit the board. Compute the
90	  product once in a build-time patch (`tools/celtic_patch.py`). Map any libm
91	  call the hack makes that `single_precision.h` does not (`rint`, `floor`),
92	  and check the object with `nm` for `__*df*` helpers, not only `__muldf3`.
93	
94	## Slow hack
95	
96	When: a ported hack runs under about 10 fps and the push is not the cause
97	(`step` in the serial line is large).
98	
99	- For a GL hack, flash a `-DGL_PROFILE` build first (AGENTS.md): it splits
100	  the frame into stages, and time in none of them is the hack's own code.
101	  Issue #73 guessed Hypnowheel was 70 percent blended fill; the profile showed
102	  a third of its frame was `double` trig.
103	- A worst-case microbenchmark is not the workload. A PSRAM cache miss costs
104	  about 220 cycles, which suggested GL fill was memory-bound; a banded renderer
105	  in internal RAM, built on that, was exact and slower (neighbouring triangles
106	  share cache lines). A/B the first working slice of a speed idea on the board
107	  before building the rest, and stop if it does not pay.
108	- Do not trust a host profile (`sample` on the dump program) for where the
109	  time goes. A Mac does `double` at full speed, so software-double code looks
110	  cheap there: Braid's disc fill was 6% on the host and the largest cost on the
111	  board.
112	- Split the step on the device with a temporary build flag that makes the
113	  expensive call return at once (Braid: `XDrawLine`). The step left is the
114	  hack's own cost; the difference is the drawing. Remove the flag before
115	  committing.
116	- Count what is called per frame (segments, calls, rows) before guessing,
117	  and look at the object file for soft-double helpers (see "Single precision").
118	- Change one thing, pin that the pixels did not move (`cmp` frames at several
119	  counts, or the pinned hash), flash, and compare second windows. Braid's four
120	  changes were worth 2.7-3.2 times, 1.05, and 1.3.
121	- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1) are the costly path: a quad filled a row at
122	  a time, plus two discs for round caps. `stroke.c` keeps a table of disc rows
123	  by width up to 16. A wide full circle through `XDrawArc` is about a thousand
124	  such segments (Deluxe: 94% of a frame, 2-5 fps); `stroke_circle` fills it as
125	  a ring in two spans a row.
126	- When the cost is overpaint, not `double` maths, a host split does find the
127	  dominant call: `#define XDrawArc(...) 0` in the wrapper, `pio run -e dump`,
128	  then `/usr/bin/time -p .pio/build/dump/program <index> 400 out.raw` three
129	  times, against the baseline. It cannot see costs that live in memory
130	  traffic (Deluxe's alpha mask: nothing on the host, 3-5 ms on the board).
131	- Counting works where timing misleads: a scratch copy of the hack with a
132	  counter in the inner function and a macro round `XDrawLine` gave Celtic's
133	  spline evaluations and line draws per draw call on the host, by graph type.
134	  A cost per eval and per line fitted to a first device capture (about 1.7 us
135	  and 22 us, from three graph types and a handful of windows) estimated 63 ms
136	  for the biggest type after the change; the next capture's 12.6-76.8 ms did
137	  not contradict it, but the log does not say which type each window was, so
138	  the fit is unchecked.
139	- A hack's own pacing constants can be the lever: Celtic's 0.0001 tick (a
140	  patch scales it, `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE`) set both the look-ahead's work and how
141	  many draw calls a picture takes. Count the draw calls a picture takes and
142	  the pause after it before reading `fps=`: with a 5 s pause the column read
143	  5.2 in every window and measured the pause, not the drawing. Use
144	  `1000 / (step + push + delay)` for the drawing rate.
145	- Heap and speed were two problems in Celtic and one fix cured only the
146	  first: the graph sized to the screen cut a pattern's heap about 9 times and
147	  left spline evaluations per call unchanged. Measure both after each change.
148	- A hack that redraws its whole picture every frame to animate colour (Braid)
149	  costs its full draw each frame whatever the push does. Check this before
150	  porting; the scorer does not flag it yet.
151	- A fix that moves the frame rate by under 5% shows the maths was not the
152	  cost. HexTrail in single precision went from 12.7 to 13.0 fps; the 2.3 fps
153	  that mattered came from reading what the GL layer does each frame
154	  (`glshim_clear`) and finding a depth clear that nothing read, because the hack
155	  never enables the depth test. Run `nm` on the object, then read the shared
156	  code the hack calls before trying a third idea in the hack.
157	- A step that grows over the hack's cycle (HexTrail: 19 ms to a ceiling, then it
158	  restarts) needs the worst window, not the mean. Capture at least one full
159	  cycle (150 s covered HexTrail's 65 s), read the lowest `fps=`, and compare the
160	  time spent below 10 fps with the rotation interval: Rod saw it fall under 10
161	  before the 25 s change. If a resource such as `count` scales the cost, give it
162	  an `#ifndef` default in `registry.c` (`HEXTRAIL_COUNT`) so one flash tests
163	  another value, and measure two or three values: count 6 gave a mean of 12.7,
164	  10 gave 9.1 and 20 gave 5.7, in double precision.
165	- Before writing a speed override, grep the hack's header and glue for the
166	  author's own knob (`GLB_SLOW_GL` in `bubble3d.h`, set from the wrapper with
167	  `#undef` and `#define` after the header). It keeps the copy byte-identical
168	  and is the trade the author intended: Bubble3D went from 4-5 fps to a mean
169	  of 11.4. A hack split over several files (entry point in one, work in
170	  another) gets one `<name>_*gl.c` wrapper per file, and only the file that
171	  does the maths needs `single_precision.h`.
172	
173	## Thin lines in a GL hack
174	
175	When: a GL hack draws hairlines or fades (Unknown Pleasures) and looks right
176	in a host frame but flickers on the board. Work down this list, one layer at a
177	time, and look at the screen (or film) after each; each layer hid the next.
178	
179	- Lines hop. TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel, so a drifting line
180	  jumps. `tinygl_patch.py` keeps the fractional position and draws a Wu line
181	  when the hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Triangles are still snapped.
182	- Quads that hide the lines behind them hide nothing, or the picture is
183	  speckled grey. TinyGL's blend adds colours, ignores alpha and misreads our
184	  byte-swapped pixels, so `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA` is drawn as an
185	  opaque fill. Smooth lines carry no alpha, so a hack's per-line fade is lost.
186	- A line drawn on its own polygon's edge is erased in dashes: `glPolygonOffset`
187	  was stored and never read. The patch applies it, plus a margin for the
188	  vertex snapping. Check the effect on the host by the second difference of a
189	  frame's total brightness while the picture drifts a fraction of a pixel; change
190	  one thing at a time, because blending once made the experiment unable to
191	  show any effect.
192	- Pieces of a line vanish for one refresh. The panel scans while the push
193	  writes, so a seam crosses the picture. Set `sync_to_refresh` on the hack
194	  (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`); see `.claude/rules/device-display.md` for the
195	  offset, why it is only valid for a full-frame push, and how to film the
196	  result. Cost: up to a refresh of latency a frame, so only a hack that needs
197	  it should ask.
198	- Budget with `gl_budget.py` but expect it to be off: it has no blend term
199	  (Unknown Pleasures was predicted at 251 ms and ran at 267, then 197 once the
200	  fills were opaque). Add the measured row as a calibration point.
201	- After all that a dimming of about 14% for 25 ms at each push remained (issue
202	  #68). Do not promise a hack is flicker-free from a host frame or from the
203	  absence of vanishing lines alone.
204	
205	## Stack check
206	
207	When: locals over a few KB. Compile the hack with `-O1 -fstack-usage` (flags in
208	AGENTS.md) and keep each frame well under the 16 KB loop stack. Host tests
209	cannot see an overflow: Rorschach's 9.6 KB array rebooted the device on its
210	first frame, and only the serial log's "Stack canary" showed it.
211	
212	Recursion: replay it, don't guess. Run the hack on a pthread with a painted
213	1 MB stack over several seeds and thousands of frames (Pacman's generator: 236
214	KB median, 315 KB worst; `ulimit -s` saw only the first, shallow level). Read a
215	frame's size from the ELF (`xtensa-esp32s3-elf-objdump -d`, `entry a1, N`), and
216	decode a panic backtrace with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-addr2line` against an ELF
217	rebuilt with the same flags. A recursion over a grid is bounded by its cells:
218	replay it from every start.
219	
220	## Large allocations
221	
222	When: one allocation of 100 KB or more, or the hack calls `exit()` if it fails.
223	
224	- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so host leak
225	  numbers are double the device's.
226	- Plain `malloc` and `realloc` of two 868 KB buffers (Substrate) landed in
227	  PSRAM: free PSRAM fell by 1,742,096 bytes, which is 2 x 466 x 466 x 4 plus a
228	  few KB. Internal heap barely moved.
229	- On restart the buffers were freed and allocated again, and free PSRAM
230	  returned to the same value. Read heap and PSRAM in the log to confirm this
231	  for each large hack.
232	
233	## Images
234	
235	Colour pixmaps are canvases: every drawing primitive, `XCopyArea` and
236	`XCopyPlane` draw into them. Bitmaps take only `XCopyArea` from another
237	bitmap. There is no PNG
238	decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads a raw RGB565 blob and
239	mask (format in `ximage-loader.h`), made by `tools/make_logo_blob.py`.
240	`XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repository root) swaps the logo for a local
241	image at build time. Keep a third-party logo under `vendor/`, out of git.
242	
243	A big blob (Pacman's is 3 MB as C text) is built from `vendor/` by a `pre:`
244	script and never committed; write it to a `.partial` file and rename it.
245	
246	## Pixmap double buffering
247	
248	When: a plain screenhack makes two pixmaps, draws into them and `XCopyArea`s the
249	result to the window (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes, Halftone,
250	Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole). Since #61 this works as copied, but a back
251	buffer costs 434 KB of PSRAM and a full-frame copy each frame, and dirties
252	every row, so the push loses what the dirty rectangle (#52) saves. Draw
253	straight on the canvas instead, as below. (These eight were ported before #61,
254	when the copy from a blank pixmap erased the picture.)
255	
256	- A pinned hash of a blank frame passes silently (`0xa4f79500bd791711ull`, which
257	  is also Pedal's at frame 200). Look at the frame before pinning.
258	- Upstream switches the buffering off under `HAVE_JWXYZ` ("Don't second-guess
259	  Quartz's double-buffering"), or reads a `doubleBuffer` resource. Write
260	  `hacks/<name>_direct.c`: include `screenhack.h` and the math headers, empty
261	  `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, `#define HAVE_JWXYZ`, include the unmodified hack and
262	  register its `HackEntry`. Exclude the original from `build_src_filter` in all
263	  three environments. `grep HAVE_JWXYZ` first: Interaggregate also uses it for
264	  pixel packing, but only in the 24 and 32 bit cases, and the canvas is 16 bit.
265	- A hack that uses a pixmap as storage needs no wrapper. Truchet draws a canvas
266	  bigger than the window into an 866 by 866 pixmap (1.5 MB of PSRAM) and
267	  scrolls it with `XCopyArea` offsets.
268	
269	## Restart leak test
270	
271	When: the hack restarts itself. Override its cycle resource in the test (for
272	example `*maxCycles: 3`), compare `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes()`
273	before and after many restarts, and prove the test sees a leak by removing a
274	`free` in a temporary copy or leaking from a shim function. Never leave the
275	hack changed: `cmp` it afterwards.
276	
277	Measure the growth first, then set the tolerance just above it (Pacman: exactly
278	0, so 512 bytes). A loose one passes a leaked GC; mutation-check by leaking one.
279	
280	On the device, work out how long a restart takes: cycles times the frame time.
281	Substrate's 10,000 cycles at about 160 ms is 27 minutes, and the restart showed
282	at about 25. Capture that long, with `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`.
283	
284	## Stopping before the first draw
285	
286	When: the hack allocates on its first `draw` (look for a lazy `initted` flag)
287	but sizes its `free` from values set in `init`. Two quick button presses, or a
288	press with the 90 s rotation, free a hack before it has drawn once. Blaster
289	sets `NUM_ROBOTS` in init, allocates `robots` in draw, and its free loops over
290	`robots[i].lasers`, so freeing it first dereferenced NULL. The dump tool with 0
291	frames exited 139.
292	
293	- `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame` starts and stops every
294	  hack with no frame, so a new port that has this problem fails the host suite.
295	- To fix it without editing the hack, write a wrapper that includes the
296	  unmodified source with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers the hack
297	  itself, with a `free` that makes the loop safe (`hacks/blaster_safe.c`).
298	- A real press is rarely handled in that window: Rod's presses on the device
299	  all landed after the first step. Rely on the test, not on pressing buttons.
300	- An xlockmore hack cannot be re-registered that way: `xlockmore.h` has no
301	  include guard, so the hack's own include redefines `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`
302	  after the wrapper empties it. Swap the callback in the table instead, from a
303	  constructor: `<name>_xlockmore_function_table.hack_init = my_init;`
304	  (`loop_direct.c`, `hypnowheel_single_gl.c`).
305	
306	## Tests that cannot be fooled
307	
308	A test that runs a real hack can pass for the wrong reason. Pyro clears its own
309	window in `init`, so a "starts black" test through Pyro passed with the runner
310	deliberately broken. Test shared runner behaviour with stub hacks
311	(`test_runner_xsft.c`) and mutate the code to see the test fail.
312	
313	A check can also be true before the hack has run. "At least 20 non-black
314	pixels" proved a hack drew, until Substrate started on a white canvas and
315	passed without drawing at all. Compare with the canvas as the hack started, and
316	keep a stub hack that draws nothing, on the colour that fooled the old check, to
317	show the test can fail. When a change alters what every hack starts with (the
318	background colour, an initial canvas), re-read the older tests that assume the
319	old start.
320	
321	A bounds guard can be unreachable through the public API. TinyGL's clipper
322	keeps a line inside the view volume and its viewport maps that to at most pixel
323	63.5, so two of the four guards in the smooth-line plot survived mutation until
324	a test used a viewport bigger than the canvas. Mutate each guard on its own
325	(a scratchpad script that edits, runs the suite and restores in `finally`),
326	and when one survives, find an input that reaches it or say it is defensive.
327	Wrapping bugs can also hide in what is stored, not what is drawn: a depth that
328	wrapped round only showed when a third fill was drawn afterwards.
329	
330	## Wrapping an xlockmore hack's init or draw
331	
332	Emptying `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` (Blaster) fails: the hack includes
333	`xlockmore.h`, which has no include guard and defines it again. Rename the
334	hack's tables instead (`#define pipes_xscreensaver_function_table
335	pipes_upstream_xscreensaver_table`, the same for `_xlockmore_function_table`),
336	include the hack, `#undef` both, define the wrappers, then
337	`#define draw_pipes pipes_draw_no_fade` and call
338	`XSCREENSAVER_MODULE_2("Pipes", pipes, pipes)`. See `hacks/pipes_gl.c`.
339	
340	## Background colour
341	
342	The runner paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before `init`,
343	as `screenhack.c` paints the window. Substrate (`.background: white`) depends
344	on it. Every earlier hack asks for black or nothing.
345	
346	## Skipping a hack
347	
348	Threads and shared memory are not worth porting. Record the name and the
349	reason in `tools/failed_ports.txt` (`name: reason`); the scorer marks it as
350	abandoned. Xft text used to be on this list; it is not now (see "Xft text").
351	
352	## Xft text
353	
354	A hack that draws with Xft (`XftDrawStringUtf8`, `load_xft_font_retry`) needs
355	the stand-in in `x11shim/xft.h`. Its font is Special Elite, rasterised at build
356	time into pixel-coverage tables (`firmware/font_atlas.py`, which runs
357	`tools/make_font_atlas.py` on the TTF in `firmware/assets/fonts/`), and
358	`main.cpp` installs it with `xshim_set_font`. Only ASCII has glyphs: anything
359	else draws as `?`. The family in a font name is ignored and the baked size
360	nearest the number is used, so to change a hack's text size override its font
361	resource (XJack's `XJACK_FONT_PX`) and bake the size in `font_atlas.py`.
362	
363	Our `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, because that would change what
364	every hack sees. Build the hack through a wrapper that includes it first
365	(`hacks/xjack_xft.c`), and exclude the original from all three
366	`build_src_filter` lines. XJack's wrapper shows two things an Xft hack may
367	need from `screenhack.c`: the window background set from the `background`
368	resource (`XClearWindow` otherwise clears to black), and a reshape after
369	init. Tests that run the hack install `test_font.h`'s blocky font, so a
370	pinned hash does not follow FreeType; with no font installed the shim gives a
371	blank one, so a test that replays every hack does not abort.
372	
373	## Worktree setup
374	
375	A fresh worktree lacks the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/`:
376	symlink them from the main checkout. They show as untracked, so `git add`
377	named paths, never `-A`. Adding them to `.git/info/exclude` changes state shared
378	with every worktree: ask Rod first.
379	
380	A worktree session refuses `source`, `$VAR` in a command and `&&` chains with a
381	computed path. Run plain commands with literal paths, for example
382	`PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio test -e native`.
383	
384	## Device capture
385	
386	- Pin the hack with `-DSTART_HACK=\"name\"` and add `-DROTATE_SECONDS=0`, or the
387	  board rotates to the next hack after 90 s.
388	- Send upload output to a file, never through `head`, and look for "Hash of
389	  data verified".
390	- Capture 150 s or more of serial in the background, longer to see a restart.
391	  Read `step`, `push`, `wait`, heap and PSRAM, and any "Stack canary".
392	- Compare with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: pushes became
393	  41-45 ms on every hack after the byte-order fix, against 31 ms before (#23).
394	- Pinning a frame hash: set the new hack's `kBaseline` entry to `1`, run
395	  `pio test -f test_hacks`, read `Was N` in the failure and convert with
396	  `python3 -c "print('0x%016xull' % N)"`. Pin only after looking at the frame
397	  (and never type the hex by hand: one was wrong).
398	- Showing Rod a hack: flash `-DSTART_HACK=\"first\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=25` with
399	  `XS_LOGO=...` so the new ones come up in order, then tell him which, and that
400	  the button steps backwards (from Pyro it wraps to the last hack).

2	
3	Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.
4	
5	The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
6	hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:
7	
8	1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
9	   read its licence header.
10	2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
11	   it fail. Add `test_<name>_stops_do_not_leak` beside the others, and
12	   mutation-check it: remove each free a wrapper adds and watch it fail.
13	3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
14	   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
15	4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
16	   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
17	5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
18	   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
19	   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
20	   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
21	   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again. A new hack never gets
22	   `0` in `kBaseline`: `0` is for a hack left unpinned on purpose, with the
23	   reason in its comment (DecayScreen, RotZoomer).
24	6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
25	   `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
26	   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
27	   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
28	   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
29	   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
30	   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
31	7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
32	   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
33	   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
34	   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
35	   counts. A resource
36	   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
37	   leak-test any override.
38	8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
39	   and came back through issue #37): remove it
40	   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
41	   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
42	   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
43	   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
44	   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
45	   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
46	   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back
47	   to.
48	   Unhook its build steps too: its entry in `patch_float_literals.py` and any
49	   pre-script only it needs (BlockTube's `gl_textures.py`), or every build
50	   still runs them and fails without their `vendor/` input.
51	9. A header that a pre-script writes into the build dir (the font, the grab
52	   image) must be included under `__has_include` in `native/dump_main.c`:
53	   `tools/probe_hacks.py` compiles that file without the build's generated
54	   directory, and an unconditional include failed two `test_probe_hacks`
55	   cases. Add the pre-script to all three `extra_scripts` lines in
56	   `platformio.ini`, and a wrapper's original source to all three
57	   `build_src_filter` lines (`sed -i.bak 's|<last entry>$|<last entry> <new>|'`

22	# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas
23	
24	OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
25	`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.
26	
27	- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
28	  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
29	  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
30	  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
31	  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
32	  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
33	- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
34	  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
35	  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
36	  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
37	  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
38	  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
39	  `normals.h` define clashing types.
40	- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
41	  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
42	  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
43	- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
44	  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
45	  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
46	  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
47	- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
48	  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
49	  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
50	  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
51	  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
52	  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
53	- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
54	  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
55	  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
56	  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
57	- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
58	  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
59	  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
60	- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
61	  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
62	- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
63	  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
64	  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
65	- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
66	  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
67	  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
68	  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
69	  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
70	  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
71	  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
72	  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
73	  new hack for both.
74	- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
75	  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
76	  neither.
77	- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
78	  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
79	  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
80	  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
81	  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
82	  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
83	- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
84	  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
85	  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
86	  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
87	- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
88	  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
89	  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
90	  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
91	  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
92	  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
93	  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
94	  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
95	  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
96	  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
97	  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
98	  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
99	- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
100	  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
101	  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
102	  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
103	  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
104	  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
105	  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
106	  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
107	  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
108	  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
109	  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
110	  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
111	  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
112	  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
113	- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
114	  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
115	  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
116	  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
117	  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
118	  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
119	  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
120	- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
121	  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
122	  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
123	  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
124	  to reach them.
125	- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
126	  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
127	  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
128	  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
129	  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
130	  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
131	  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
132	  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
133	  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
134	- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
135	  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
136	  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
137	- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
138	  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
139	  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
140	- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
