167	  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
168	  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is integer now
169	  (see `x11shim.md`; Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
170	  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
171	  canvas lacks.
172	- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
173	  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
174	  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
175	  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
176	  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
177	  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
178	  pixel-identical by construction;
179	  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
180	  screen.
181	- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
182	  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
183	  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
184	  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
185	  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
186	  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
187	  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
188	  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
189	  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
190	  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
191	  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
192	  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
193	  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
194	  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.
195	- Loop asks for 100 ms between generations (8.7 fps with a 3.5-7 ms step); the
196	  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
197	  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
198	  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
199	  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
200	  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
201	  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
202	  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
203	  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
204	  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
205	  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
206	  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
207	  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
208	  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
209	- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
210	  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
211	  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
212	  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
213	  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
214	  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
215	  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
216	- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
217	  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
218	  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
219	  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
220	  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
221	  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
222	  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
223	  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
224	  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
225	- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
226	  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
227	  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
228	  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
229	  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
230	- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
231	  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
232	  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
233	  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
234	  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
235	  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
236	  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
237	  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
238	  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
239	  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
240	  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
241	- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
242	  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
243	  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
244	  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
245	  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
246	  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
247	  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
248	  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
249	  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
250	  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
251	  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
252	  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
253	  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
254	  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
255	- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
256	  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md.in`).
257	  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
258	  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
259	  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
260	  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
261	  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
262	  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
263	  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
264	  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
265	  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
266	  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
267	  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
268	  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
269	  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
270	  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
271	  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
272	  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
273	  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
274	  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
275	  comes out too small to fill the screen.
276	- A full-frame write to the PSRAM canvas costs about 25 ms whatever does it
277	  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
278	  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
279	  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
280	  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
281	  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
282	  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
283	  at 10.2 fps.
284	- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
285	  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
286	  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
287	- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`
288	  (67 to 42 ms) and frees each circle's high fringe, which upstream's free
289	  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).
290	- BinaryRing (`binaryring_single.c`) is told the display is 24 bits deep: its
291	  16-bit path drops every hit below one 5-bit step, so only green builds up
292	  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
293	  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:
294	  the 32-bit image was put a pixel at a time, 130 of a 240 ms step.
295	  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.
296	- GraphStat's word list (`graphstat.h`) is copied from `vendor/` at build
297	  time (`firmware/vendor_data.py`); since 6.17 upstream ships the header, each
298	  word wrapped in `_()` for `gettext` (`x11shim/include/nls.h`). Its timing
299	  is in frames tuned for 30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s
300	  instead of 12.
301	- EtruscanVenus (`etruscanvenus_single_gl.c`) runs on a 48 by 32 grid
302	  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;
303	  `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU`, `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV` and `-DETRUSCANVENUS_FULL`
304	  try others. Its modes differ: those that fill the screen are fill-bound.
305	  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).
306	- BlockTube was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and not much going on);
307	  its source, notices row, `blocktube_single_gl.c`, `gl_textures.py` and
308	  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring
309	  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and
310	  `blocktube` (with its `count_the_blocks`) to `patch_float_literals.py`
311	  again. It drew 400 blocks
312	  (`tools/blocktube_patch.py`, upstream's 1,000) at half resolution with a
313	  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
314	  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
315	  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
316	  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
317	  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters
318	  `glEnable` of fog and texture generation, which TinyGL warns about every
319	  frame.
320	- Companion Cube and Floppy are not ported (Rod dropped both, listed in
321	  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
322	  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
323	  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
324	  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).
325	- Rocks and DecayScreen were wired, looked at and dropped in the 2026-10-12
326	  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
327	  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
328	  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
329	  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
330	  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it
331	  runs at 17.2 fps against its own 50 ms delay, and holds 2.66 MB of PSRAM and
332	  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
333	  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
334	  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
335	  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
336	  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
337	  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
338	  with.
339	- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
340	  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
341	  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
342	  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
343	  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
344	- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
345	  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
346	  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
347	  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
348	  all looked at).
349	- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
350	  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
351	  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
352	  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
353	  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
354	  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
355	  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
356	  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.
357	- XJack (`xjack_xft.c`) types "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" in
358	  Special Elite on cream paper, through the Xft stand-in. Its first host frames
359	  were black (it clears the window, and the shim cleared to black) and then
360	  half-drawn lines scrolled in from the bottom (`xjack_init` sizes the page
361	  before its 40 pixel margins, and xscreensaver reshapes it after): the wrapper
362	  sets the window background and calls `xjack_reshape`, and each has a test
363	  that fails without it. Upstream's `font2` of 12 is small on a 466 pixel
364	  panel: Rod found 16 small and 20 good, so the wrapper overrides it to 20
365	  (`-DXJACK_FONT_PX=<12|16|20|24>`; about 28 columns). The margins swing
366	  (modes 1 to 4 walk them diagonally on purpose), and the round bezel cuts the
367	  corners of the page. Rod has seen it on the panel. It runs at 8-16 fps, set
368	  by its own delay (`wait` is 46-130 ms): typing is a 0.1 ms step, scrolling
369	  3.9-13.8 ms with pushes of 74-241 rows. It holds no PSRAM, and a 6-minute
370	  capture lost 352 bytes of internal heap in three steps (see
371	  `assessment_measured.md.in`).
372	- The 2026-10-13 sixth batch (Marbling, Deco, IMSMap, MetaBalls, Munch, CCurve,
373	  BinaryHorizon, RotZoomer, Twang, NerveRot, Flow, Bouboule, Ant, HyperBall,
374	  Demon, Droste, Polyominoes, Barcode) passed every host test and then four
375	  of them failed on the board, none of which a host frame could show: a stack
376	  overflow (Polyominoes), an allocation too big for PSRAM that the host's lazy
377	  memory allowed (Flow), 0.6 fps (Marbling) and 1.6 fps (Droste). Flash a
378	  batch before calling it done. A rotation build starting at the first new
379	  hack (`-DSTART_HACK=\"marbling\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=30`) measures all of them
380	  in one 10 minute capture. Rod then took MetaBalls, Twang, Flow and Droste
381	  out of `g_hacks[]` (slow or margin-bound, not worth tuning). Their sources,
382	  wrappers and wrapper tests stay in the tree, unregistered; to bring one
383	  back, re-add its registry entry, expected name, pin and leak test.
384	- Marbling does a 5-iteration fractal noise per pixel (12 ms a step on the
385	  host, 1,785 ms on the board, so the host suite takes about 3 minutes
386	  longer). `marbling_safe.c` overrides `*gridsize` to 6 and `*iterations` to 3
387	  (5.4 fps, cells of 6 pixels). Upstream's `marbling_free` never frees its
388	  colour table (5 KB a start): the wrapper does.
389	- Polyominoes (`polyominoes_iterative.c`, `tools/polyominoes_patch.py`) panicked
390	  the board with a double exception inside `count_adjacent_blanks`: a flood
391	  fill that calls itself once for each blank cell, up to 360 deep in several
392	  puzzles, 32 bytes a level on top of the solver's frames. The build now
393	  replaces it with a loop over an explicit stack (frames identical to the
394	  recursive build). Read a puzzle hack's grid sizes, not just its frame size.
395	- Flow's `csegs` is `(count + 36) * ncolors * taillen` segments of 8 bytes:
396	  upstream's 3,000 bees and 200 colours is up to 29 MB, which the host
397	  provided lazily and the board refused, so the hack drew one frame and
398	  nothing more. The registry gives it 120 bees and 8 colours. In single
399	  precision its flow dies out within about 600 frames (the screen stays
400	  black), so it is double: 3.0-4.8 fps, about 200 ms of every step being its
401	  search for the next flow. A single frame at 300 frames looked right in
402	  both: sweep several frame counts (300, 1000, 3000) for a hack that
403	  restarts itself or can die out.
404	- CCurve's `*limit` of 200,000 segments (each a malloc and a recursion) took
405	  740 ms in single precision and 2.9 s in double; the wrapper caps it at 30,000.
406	  Its 1.4 fps is its own pacing: 0.4 s between iterations, 42 ms of work.
407	- Droste (`droste_small.c`) hands back a loader token on the first call and
408	  finishes on the next, with the pixmap's size as the rectangle, so upstream's
409	  own "just finished" branch runs. It loads a picture the size of the window,
410	  not 2.5 times it (5.4 MB as the 32-bit image `XGetImage` makes), and renders
411	  at half width and height through `lowrez_put.h` (630 ms became 190 ms, 4.6
412	  fps). `XPutPixel` is mapped to swap the pixel, since `lowrez_put.h` wants
413	  ordinary RGB565 and the picture holds canvas order. MetaBalls takes all but
414	  28 KB of the internal heap while it runs (466 row buffers of 466 bytes).
415	- RotZoomer and Twang (`rotzoomer_single.c`, `twang_single.c`) start their
416	  picture and tiles the first time `draw` finds `load_image_async_simple`
417	  finished. The shim finishes at once and returns NULL, so that branch never
418	  ran and the first draw used a NULL zoom box (exit 139). Each wrapper does
419	  the finishing step straight after init. Changing the shim to return a loader
420	  would also change Boxfit and DecayScreen, so it is Rod's call. Both are
421	  single precision (they call `sin` and `cos` in double for every pixel).
422	  RotZoomer is unpinned in `test_hacks.c`: with no grab image every frame is
423	  black.
424	- BinaryHorizon (`binaryhorizon_swapped.c`) is told the display is 24 bits
425	  deep. Its 16-bit path adds less than a step of a channel per hit and rounds
426	  its random colour walk down, so every colour drifted to black or a dim
427	  green (as in BinaryRing). Pixels go straight to the window, and its image
428	  and pixmap are one pixel big, because nothing reads them. Every 30 s it
429	  restarts and callocs a new pixel buffer without freeing the old one (868 KB
430	  on the device): the wrapper frees it and clears the window.
431	- Munch defaults to `*xor: True`, so `XDrawPoint` honours `GXxor` now (only
432	  that primitive: lines and fills still copy). `pow2.h` is our own
433	  `i_log2` and `to_pow2`. IMSMap needed 1-bit `XYBitmap` images, `BitmapPad`
434	  is 32, and Deco needed `allocate_writable_colors` and `XStoreColors` (no
435	  writable cells). The scorer's gap lists were wrong twice: MetaBalls'
436	  `XListPixmapFormats` is under `#if 0`, and Ant needed only `automata.h`, a
437	  file in `hacks/` that is now copied to `xs_support/`.
438	- NerveRot passes the address of its own `double` locals to `rgb_to_hsv`, so
439	  its single-precision wrapper has an adapter (as Moire's). The restart test
440	  under AddressSanitizer found it as a stack-buffer-overflow, but a host frame
441	  looked right.
442	- Bouboule's upstream default is a red and a blue starfield for 3D glasses,
443	  drawn with `GXor`, which the shim does not do. The registry overrides
444	  `*use3d: False` (a single colour cycling through the palette) and
445	  `*cycles: 0`. Twang's 3 by 3 tiles of 120 pixels leave black margins and
446	  clip at the round bezel; `*tileSize` is the lever.
447	- A wrapper that finishes an image load itself (RotZoomer, Twang, Droste) must
448	  also handle the hack's timed reload, which the shim finishes at once too, so
449	  upstream's "just finished" branch never runs again. It must also match image
450	  layouts: `XGetImage` gives a 32-bit image, and a hack that memcpys it into
451	  its own 16-bit buffer shows alternating black pixels. RotZoomer did on the
452	  board until the trail review caught it. Test with a flat grab image and
453	  assert every pixel, then change the image before a timed restart.
454	- A wrapper that clears state before upstream's own timed check (BinaryHorizon
455	  frees its buffer) reads the clock separately from upstream, and the two reads
456	  can straddle a second. Read it once a frame and route upstream's `time()` to
457	  that reading with a function-like `#define time(p)`; test it with a fake
458	  clock whose second read is later.
459	- A hack that leaks on every in-hack restart (Munch's `get_string_resource`
460	  result) needs a restart-loop leak test of its own: `test_hacks` restarts only
461	  through start and stop.
462	- Deluxe's `draw_star` (ten sin/cos in software `double`, #54 idea 5): a
463	  single-precision build gave identical frames and no device gain (step
464	  45.06 vs 45.12 ms, pinned, 2 rounds). Skip it; the step is the blend, the
465	  mask and the strokes.
466	- Bubble3D is four files (`b_lockglue.c` holds `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`, so the
467	  scorer knows it as `b_lockglue`; `SOURCE_STEMS` in `score_hacks.py` maps the
468	  registry name `bubble3d` to it), each built as its own `USE_GL` unit by
469	  `bubble3d_*gl.c`. Only `bubble3d.c` has a licence text; Rod chose to list the
470	  other four under its notice. The glue's `init()` builds a sphere and drops it
471	  (leaked on every start: the wrapper makes that call return NULL). A GL
472	  profile put 220 of a 300-390 ms step in a software-double `cos` per nudge
473	  axis per vertex: `bubble3d_bubble_gl.c` is single precision (frames
474	  byte-identical). Upstream's own `GLB_SLOW_GL` (set in `bubble3d_gl.c`) takes
475	  the sphere from 1,280 to 320 triangles: 4-5 fps became mean 11.5, worst
476	  window 8.2, with the push (12-24 ms, a full frame) now a fifth of the frame.
477	  It is flagged `repaints_all` since the GL layer follows the canvas swap
478	  (issue #118): 11.2 to 12.0 fps, worst window 8.0 to 8.8. Upstream's
479	  default `transparent` skips the depth test and expects a blend TinyGL's fill
480	  does not do, so back faces overwrote front faces as a dark wedge in each
481	  bubble (found by the trail review): the registry overrides `*transparent:
482	  False`, which enables the depth test. It cost nothing measurable on the
483	  board (mean 11.5 before, 11.4 after).
484	- Bubbles (`bubbles_safe.c`, `bubbles_sprites.py`) is three copied files and
485	  44 PNGs (four sets of eleven sizes: blood, blue, glass, jade) that the
486	  pre-script deflates into the build dir with `make_logo_blob.py --deflate`,
487	  never committed. Upstream's free leaks every live bubble in the mesh lists
488	  and one extra step pixmap: the wrapper frees both, and the leak test fails
489	  if either free is removed (checked by mutation). `bubbles.h` includes
490	  `<X11/Xlib.h>`, which the shim now answers with a header that pulls in
491	  `xshim.h`. A host dump always shows the same set, so seed `random()` to see
492	  the others (jade, blue and glass came up in six seeds, blood did not).
493	  Blood is teal with red mottling in the source art, not red: Rod saw cyan
494	  with red spots on the panel and it matches `blood11.png`, so it is not a
495	  byte swap. A single frame can show a bubble with a bite out of it while
496	  neighbours merge and are redrawn; the bite is gone a few frames later. On
497	  the board it ran at 54-62 fps (mean 57.4), a 5-7 ms step under its own
498	  9.5 ms wait, and held nothing in PSRAM: it is paced by its delay, not by the
499	  work.

329	- `tools/wire_hack.py` puts a new hack before the After Dark toasters'
330	  `#ifdef` in the registry, the expected list and `kBaseline`.
331	- Added for the 2026-10-12 second batch, each test-first: `XClearArea` (the
332	  window background, clipped; a width or height of 0 runs to the window's
333	  edge; Worm), `XMaxRequestSize` (65535, so Lisa batches about 32,000 points a
334	  call) and the `LineOnOffDash` and `LineDoubleDash` constants (accepted;
335	  lines still draw solid; Penrose uses them only in its monochrome path). The
336	  scorer's gap list was wrong for Triangle (`free_colors` and
337	  `make_smooth_colormap` exist; its xlockmore include chain just does not
338	  reach `colors.h`, so `hacks/triangle_colors.c` includes `screenhack.h`
339	  first) and XRaySwarm (`initTime` is the hack's own, behind
340	  `HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY`, which upstream takes from `config.h`:
341	  `hacks/xrayswarm_time.c` defines it). Putting `colors.h` in the shim's
342	  `screenhackI.h` would have fixed Triangle for all but changes what every
343	  xlockmore hack sees, so it is Rod's call.
344	- `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` fill a depth-1 pixmap now (Rocks): a bit
345	  is set where the GC's foreground is odd and cleared where it is even, and the
346	  clip mask and the GC's function are ignored. The polygon is even-odd, a pixel
347	  being in when its centre is, in float. Other primitives still draw nothing on
348	  a bitmap. Halo, Moire2 and Goop keep their own planes or layers and did not
349	  move.
350	- `xshim_set_grab_image` (`grabclient.h`) gives `load_image_async_simple` a
351	  picture to paint over its target the next time a load starts: scaled to cover
352	  and cropped evenly at the sides (a 4:3 screenshot on the square screen loses
353	  its left and right edges), mask ignored, finishing at once as before. `main.cpp`
354	  sets it from the header `firmware/grab_image.py` writes into the build
355	  directory: `firmware/assets/grab-image.png` (Rod's choice: the Windows 95
356	  screenshot from guidebookgallery.org, committed at his say-so, with a
357	  notices section), or `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=<file>`, and `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=none` builds
358	  without. It is stored at up to 466 pixels (a 466 by 350 blob was 340
359	  KB of flash, 48 KB since it was deflated in #102: the build had gone from
360	  2.39 MB to 2.74 MB, 87.0% of the app partition). The host tests set their
361	  own picture, so a pin never depends on the local file; `dump` sets it when
362	  the header exists. DecayScreen is unpinned for that reason
363	  (`test_decayscreen_melts_the_grab_image`). Boxfit's `grab` mode, off by
364	  default, would get the picture too.
365	- `make_smooth_colormap` follows upstream's behaviour (written from scratch, not
366	  copied): two to five random points in hue, saturation and value, repicked if
367	  adjacent ones are close or the average is too grey or dark, joined in a closed
368	  path with colours spaced by edge length. The first version always spanned the
369	  hue wheel at high saturation and value, so Triangle and 23 other pinned hacks
370	  were a bright rainbow.
371	- The Xft stand-in (`xft.h`, `xft.c`, `xft_font.h`; ours) draws 8-bit coverage
372	  glyphs, blended over the canvas pixel by pixel (the canvas is byte-swapped
373	  565, so each pixel is swapped, weighed in 8-bit channels and packed again),
374	  clipped in 64 bits and marked dirty once a glyph. It ignores the GC's clip
375	  mask, as Xft does. The glyph data is baked from `assets/fonts/` at 12, 16,
376	  20 and 24 pixels (`font_atlas.py`): the tables cost about 57 KB of flash
377	  (87.0% of the app partition became 88.8% with XJack), and a size is picked
378	  by the number at the end of a font name. `screenhack.h` does not include
379	  `xft.h`: a hack gets it through a wrapper (`hacks/xjack_xft.c`). With no
380	  font installed a hack gets a blank one (advance, no ink), because XJack
381	  `abort()`s on none and `test_pyro` and `test_push_present` run every hack.
382	- The runner never sends a hack a reshape, and `XClearWindow` clears to
383	  black unless the hack calls `XSetWindowBackground`, where xscreensaver's
384	  `screenhack.c` sets the window background from the `background` resource and
385	  sends a reshape after init. A hack that depends on either needs a wrapper
386	  (XJack's `xjack_init_on_paper`); doing it in the runner would change what
387	  every hack sees, so it is Rod's call. Any other registered hack with a
388	  light `background` that calls `XClearWindow` may have the same fault.
389	- The shim's `screenhack.h` does not include `screenhackI.h` (upstream's
390	  does), so plain hacks and xlockmore hacks see different headers. Put a
391	  macro upstream defines in `screenhackI.h` for every hack into a small
392	  header both include, as `nls.h` (`_()` and `gettext`) is.

# X11 shim and framework gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `unsigned long` is 4 bytes on the device and 8 on the host, so a hack that
  allocates arrays of it (Substrate's two 466 by 466 buffers) is twice the size
  on the host, and host leak numbers are twice the device's. On the device,
  plain `malloc`/`realloc` of about 868 KB reached PSRAM (free PSRAM fell by
  1.74 MB) and came back on restart; internal heap barely moved.
- The board's `malloc` is `CONFIG_SPIRAM_USE_MALLOC=y` with
  `SPIRAM_MALLOC_ALWAYSINTERNAL=4096`: a block up to 4 KB comes from internal
  RAM and falls back to PSRAM when that is full, and a bigger one goes to PSRAM
  first. An allocation fails only when PSRAM is gone, so a hack's `abort()` on
  a failed allocation is not the risk it looks. The cost of a big pattern is
  internal heap drained to near zero (Celtic read 1,792 B free) and its data
  in slower PSRAM: compare the log's `psram=` with its idle value for the
  overflow.
- `erase_window` (`erase.c`) follows upstream's contract: the first call draws
  nothing and returns a state, so a hack that waits after it (Celtic's 5 s
  `*delay2`) waits on the finished picture. The second call starts a one-second
  wipe (blinds, circle, fizzle or random lines, picked at random), each later
  call draws the next step, and the call after the second is up clears the
  window and returns NULL. Progress comes from `double_time()`, not from the
  call count, so the wipe lasts a second at any step rate. A test or tool
  that does not sleep for a hack's delay must install a clock
  (`xshim_set_clock`), or a wipe never ends. Six hacks never call
  `eraser_free`, so the display tracks live states and the runner releases
  them when a hack stops.
- xlockmore hacks (the 40 that include `xlockmore.h`) need `-DSTANDALONE`,
  which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in
  `hacks/registry.c` with `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs
  the hack's `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of
  -2 or above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Galaxy, Drift, Discrete and Flame are built through
  `hacks/<name>_single.c`, which includes the framework headers, then
  `hacks/single_precision.h` (`double` and the libm calls become `float` and
  the `f` versions; the S3's FPU is single-precision only), then the unmodified
  hack; the original `.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.
- Wide lines (`line_width` above 1), arcs and pixmap writes live in
  `x11shim/stroke.c`, `arc.c` and `pixmap.c`. Width 0 and 1 keep the old
  `canvas_line` path, so hacks that set no wide width are pixel-identical (every
  hack's frame is pinned in `test_hacks.c`). Braid is the one registered hack
  that draws wide lines (random width 1-7; Maze's width 2 is under
  `HAVE_JWXYZ`). A round-capped segment draws a disc at each end, so
  `stroke.c` keeps each width's rows in a table (widths to 16) rather than
  calling `canvas_fill_ellipse` (which used to do `double` maths per row, in
  software on the S3; see below). A test pins the pixels to
  `canvas_fill_ellipse`.
- `canvas_fill_ellipse` and `canvas_fill_polygon` work in whole numbers, not
  double (the S3 does double in software). The ellipse is exact: a pixel is in
  when `dx2^2 * h^2 <= w^2 * (h^2 - dy2^2)` with distances doubled, and a float
  `sqrt` only starts the search for each row (it is wrong by one at 220 by 21,
  264 by 23, 312 by 25 and 318 by 181, which the tests pin). The polygon steps
  each edge's crossing with a quotient and remainder, no division per row, and
  a pixel on a left edge is in and one on a right edge is out. The old double
  fill was not consistent at exact ties (a 45 degree edge through integer
  vertices): it left stray hatch marks on Qix's thin sliver polygons, so Qix
  (612 pixels) and Pedal (3) re-pinned. Sizes or coordinates past 32768 and
  2^24 keep the double code. On the board (step, before to after): Bouboule
  14.5 to 5.2 ms (27.4 to 36.8 fps), Qix 14.6 to 1.9 ms (37.3 to 70.1 fps),
  Pedal 21.8 to 8.6 ms (it then holds the picture for 5 s).
- Lisa was the counter-example to "the stroker maths is the cost" (#98), and
  then the maths turned out to be the cost after all. Converting a slanted
  segment's ends from int to float moved it by nothing (52.1 ms either way),
  and with the line calls compiled out its step is 5.2 ms, so 47 ms of 52 was
  drawing: 1,396 segments and 6.7k spans a frame at width 2, 13k spans at
  width 8. The guess was a PSRAM cache miss per scattered span. The real
  cost was `fill_convex`: the S3 has no float divide, min, max, floor or
  64-bit conversion, so its per-row loop (two divides, `fminf`, `fmaxf`, two
  `floorf` and two `__fixsfdi` calls a row) was about 3 us a span. It now
  divides each edge's slope once per polygon and uses compares and 32-bit
  `floor_int`. That rounds a few ulps differently from dividing first, which
  moved pixels on a boundary (review of #128): a row whose span ends are within
  rounding of a boundary decision is worked out the old way, and the pixels
  match main's. Test it with each stroke on a cleared canvas
  (`test_wide_strokes_of_random_lines_match_the_pinned_hash`, pinned from main's
  rasteriser): a hash of strokes drawn together missed it, because later strokes
  covered the pixels that differed. Checking every edge of every row cost most
  of the gain (Lisa 43 ms at width 2); checking the two span ends and reusing
  their floors keeps it. On the board Lisa's step went 52.3 to 38.5 ms at width
  2 (14.2 to 17.7 fps) and 85.4 to 60.1 ms at width 8 (9.7 to 12.9 fps), Braid
  125.4 to about 94 ms (8.1 to 9.7 fps) and Deluxe 51.9 to 49.2 ms (19.0 to
  19.9 fps), two rounds each. The width
  sweep on the host (`-DLW=N` with `LINEWIDTH` edited, temporarily) shows the
  cliff is thin to wide: width 1 takes the `canvas_line` path at 0.09 ms, width
  2 is 0.52 ms and width 8 0.85 ms. Look for the same library calls in a
  per-row or per-pixel loop of any hack: `nm` on the object lists them
  (`__divsf3`, `__fixsfdi`, `floorf`, `sqrtf`).
- `canvas_line` (thin lines, width 0 and 1) keeps its endpoints as ints when
  nothing is clipped: it used to convert all four to double and back, which
  the S3 does in software, on every call. Pixels are
  unchanged (`test_lines_inside_the_canvas_match_the_reference` and the
  off-canvas twin draw 20,000 lines each, alone, with `canvas_line` and with a
  copy of the old one in the test file). Compare against a reference copy, not
  a pinned hash, for anything that goes through `clip_line`: its double
  arithmetic rounds differently when the compiler contracts to FMA, and a hash
  taken on one setting fails on the other. On the board XRaySwarm's step went
  21.05 to 13.20 ms (23.2 to 28.3 fps; about 9,700 short lines a step);
  Wormhole 26.9 to 26.0 ms and NerveRot 48.2 to 46.7 ms barely move, since
  they draw far fewer lines and clip some.
  Counting calls on the host (a scratch copy with counters in `canvas_line`,
  `arc_points`, `compute_closed_spline`) put 29 of 109 hacks on `canvas_line`.
  The colour-map builders in `helpers.c` run at start only, so their double
  maths does not matter per frame.
- `canvas_line`'s clip (`clip_line_integer`, `canvas.c`) is the Liang-Barsky
  clip in exact `int64` rationals: it compares the quotients by
  cross-multiplying and rounds each end with one integer divide. The double
  clip (`clip_line`) still decides two cases, and `canvas_line` falls back to
  it for them: an end exactly on a half pixel, where double rounding can land
  either side, and a coordinate past 2^20. The limit comes from an error bound
  (double's error stays near 1e-10, while a rational answer that is not
  exactly on a boundary is at least 1 / 2^22 from it), not from a test: a
  raised limit survives the random tests, since a miss at 10^9 is about one
  in ten million lines. A clipped end sits on the canvas border, so one
  coordinate is an integer and only the other can tie. Pixels match the old
  clip in every reference test, with FMA contraction on and off (a mutant that
  treats every integer as a tie falls back every time and so also passes). On
  the board XSpirograph's step went 11.4 to 7.45 ms (15.2 to 16.8 fps: its
  push, 18.3 to 16.3 ms, now sets the frame) with 404 of 722 lines a step
  clipped; Laser 21.3 to 20.8 ms (52% clipped, but about 270 pixels a line);
  Deco unchanged at 34.3 ms (its own delay holds it at 0.2 fps).
- `arc_points` (`arc.c`) and `compute_closed_spline` (`spline.c`) take a fast
  path and keep the old arithmetic for what the fast path cannot settle. Both
  match the old code point for point in the reference tests, with FMA
  contraction on and off; the pinned frame of every hack is unchanged.
  - `compute_closed_spline` works each point's blend of four controls in
    float (the weights are worked out once, in double, then kept as float) and
    keeps it unless it is within about 1e-3 plus 2e-6 of the largest control
    from a half pixel, where `lround` could go either way; then the original
    double expression decides. Controls past 1e6 in size take the double path
    throughout. The controls are `double` because hacks fill them in, so the
    conversion to float is once a call, not once a point. Goop: step 45.3 to
    35.4 ms (15.9 to 18.9 fps), about 500 points a step.
  - `arc_points` works a run of 16 points from the first by rotating through
    the step between points (four multiplies and two adds, not a divide, `sinf`
    and `cosf`), and a point within 2e-3 plus 4e-5 of the radius from a rounding
    boundary is worked out as before, and the rotation reseeded from it. Angles
    past 32 radians (float's spacing is then near a millionth of a radian) and
    coordinates or radii past 1e6 take the plain loop. The run length is a
    margin: the real drift over a thousand points is about 1e-3 px against a
    tolerance of 0.02 px, so a longer run passes the tests too. Piecewise:
    step 43.4 to 38.6 ms (22.4 to 25.0 fps, about 3,200 arc points a step);
    BoxFit 14.1 to 12.9 ms, with its fps flat (19.1 to 19.2) because its own
    delay sets the frame.
  - A mutant that drops the near-half fallback, one that flips a rotation
    sign, and ones that remove the angle or coordinate limits are each killed
    by the reference tests; a pinned hash would not do here either, since the
    float and double paths can round a half pixel differently.
- `single_precision.h` renames the keyword `double`, not literals: `0.5 * x`
  is still software double. Braid's wrapper includes a copy of the hack with
  every decimal literal suffixed `f`, written at build time by
  `firmware/patch_float_literals.py` (`tools/float_literals.py`). Check a
  wrapper's object for `__muldf3` and friends with `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-nm`.
  `uv run tools/softdouble_report.py <name>` does that for every object in
  the device build, by function: a count in a per-frame function is a literal
  or a macro the header could not reach. It lists none in Galaxy, Discrete,
  Drift, Flame, Substrate or Interaggregate now.
- Four things hide soft double from `single_precision.h`, each found by that
  report. `frand` (`single_frand.h`) and `MAXRAND`, `M_PI`, `M_PI_2` and
  `M_PI_4` (`single_constants.h`) are macros with a decimal literal in their
  body, past the literal pass; both headers are opt-in, since each moves the
  wrapper's frames and pins. Exponent literals (`1e-6`, `1.0E5`) were skipped
  by `float_literals.py` until Drift and Flame showed one each. A struct
  declared with `double` fields before the rename keeps them, so a float
  `corners[j].x * size` plus a `double` `pos.x` is a software add: HexTrail's
  `XYZ` (from `normals.h`) was 94 calls in `draw_hextrail`. Give the hack its
  own float struct under the same name, and `normals.h` another name for the
  double one (`hextrail_single_gl.c`; frames byte-identical). And a trig
  argument that is a big whole number cannot be a float: XSpirograph's second
  angle is millions of degrees and Vines' is an `int` in the billions, so a
  plain `double` to `float` turned both pictures to noise. XSpirograph reduces
  its angles mod 360 in integers at build time (`tools/xspirograph_patch.py`);
  Vines builds `(double) a` as `(long) a`, so its `cos` macro gets the exact
  integer and takes the phase as a 64-bit multiply by 2^64 / 2 pi, wrapping
  into whole turns (`vines_single.c`). Look at a frame before trusting a
  float build of anything whose angles grow. To find the line of a stray
  promotion, add `-Wdouble-promotion -fsyntax-only` to a file's compile
  command in `firmware/compile_commands.json` (`pio run -e stopwatch -t
  compiledb`; delete the file afterwards, it upsets the editor).
- A colour pixmap is a `Canvas`, and every drawing primitive draws on the
  drawable it is given (`xshim_target` in `pixmap.c`); `None` draws nothing,
  and a bitmap takes only `XCopyArea`, `XCopyPlane` and filled rectangles and
  polygons (see below). One exception still draws on the window whatever
  it is given: Deluxe's wrapper, which calls `stroke_circle(dpy->canvas,
  ...)`. No
  registered hack drew into a pixmap before this (the `HAVE_JWXYZ` wrappers
  and Deluxe's `doubleBuffer: False` turn double-buffering off), so keep
  those: a back buffer costs 434 KB and a full-frame copy, and dirties every
  row. Without a
  clip mask, `XCopyArea` copies colour rows whole with `canvas_paste_rect`. A
  pixmap wider or taller than `INT16_MAX` is `None` (the canvas's dirty spans
  are `int16_t`). Truchet draws into one (issue #61). The display tracks every
  pixmap a hack holds and the runner frees what a stopped hack left behind
  (Pacman leaked 514 KB per start). The GC keeps its own copy of a clip mask
  because hacks free the pixmap right after `XSetClipMask`. There is no PNG
  decoder: `image_data_to_pixmap` reads
  the raw blob described in `ximage-loader.h`, made by
  `tools/make_logo_blob.py` (`uv run`, needs Pillow). Pacman's sprites,
  XMatrix's large glyph sheets and the grab image are built with `--deflate`
  ("565Z", issue #102): 1.39 MB of flash saved, unpacked into a temporary
  buffer while the image loads (Pacman's is 522 KB of PSRAM, briefly), by the
  ROM's `tinfl` on the device and zlib on the host, so host builds link `-lz`
  (`platformio.ini`, `probe_hacks.py`, `gl_budget.py`). Host tests cover only
  zlib. XMatrix's small sheets are never drawn at 466 px: their generated
  headers `#define` them to the large ones. The `logo_180`/`360`
  headers are aliases of the 50 px data, as a 466 px screen only picks 50.
  `XS_LOGO=<image>` (relative to the repo root) swaps the logo for a local
  image, shrunk to fit 50 px, without committing it: `firmware/logo_override.py`
  writes the header into the build dir, where `maze_patched.c` finds it
  before the committed one. Unset, it deletes that header. Needs `uv`. A
  third-party logo kept under `vendor/` stays out of git that way. The WorkOS
  icon is `vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png`. A plain flash with it is
  `unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` then `XS_LOGO=vendor/workos/workos-icon-256.png
  pio run -e stopwatch -t upload`: build flags stick, so a leftover pin from
  an earlier probe would survive. The logo shows in Maze only.
- A wide circle through `XDrawArc` is a polyline of about a thousand wide
  segments, each filled a row at a time: 40 times the fills of a ring, and the
  polyline leaves gaps in it. `stroke_circle` (`x11shim/stroke.c`) fills the
  ring in two spans a row. Only Deluxe's wrapper calls it, and it does full
  circles only: Pacman's wall arcs are quarters and Celtic's wide strokes are
  lines, so they still take the stroker. The polyline's gaps were float
  rounding, not the joins or the point spacing: a pixel centre exactly on an
  edge shared by a segment quad and the join wedge at its end (any 45 degree
  edge through integer vertices) fell out of both, because float32 put the
  quad's right edge at 57.499996 for 57.5. `fill_convex` now takes a right
  edge inclusive to within `EDGE_SLACK` (1e-3; 1e-7 fails the test, 1e-5
  passes), and `test_wide_full_arc_fills_every_pixel_in_its_band` pins it. It
  moved five pinned frames by 0 to 33 pixels each (Deluxe, Forest, Rotor,
  Compass, Celtic). Pacman is not affected: its `wallwidth` is 1 at this
  size, which takes the thin-line path. Celtic's overpaint (about 50 paints a
  pixel a step on the host, 46% of its line draws zero-length) is still open
  in #56. Changing shared stroke code can move pinned frames: look at them and
  ask Rod. The pin test hashes steps 50, 100, 150 and 200 with a fake clock
  that carries across hacks, so a dump program does not reproduce its frames:
  write them from the test itself.
- `XshimGC.alpha` (0 is opaque, 1 to 31 is the weight out of 32) makes the
  wide-line code in `stroke.c` blend over the canvas instead of overwriting it;
  fills, `canvas_line` and the other primitives ignore it. The canvas is
  byte-swapped RGB565, so the blend swaps each pixel and back. A shape of
  overlapping pieces (a polyline, a round cap and its segment) sets bits in a
  mask the size of the canvas (a 27 KB `calloc` per shape, freed at the end)
  and blends it once, or the overlaps blend twice and a star's corners show
  as bright diamonds. A failed `calloc` falls back to blending piece by piece.
  Setting `alpha` takes a wrapper, as in `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `XGetImage` and `XPutImage` (`ximage.c`) move 32-bit ZPixmap images (the raw
  RGB565 value in each) to and from the window or a colour pixmap; a bitmap
  format, `None` or an empty region gives NULL. XMatrix flips its glyph sheets
  through them. Overrunning a row's right edge wraps onto the next row without
  AddressSanitizer seeing it, so a clip test must look at that next row.
- `XPutImage` copies a 16-bit image a row at a time with `memcpy`; other
  depths keep the per-pixel loop, since they keep only the low 16 bits (#82).
  ad-flyingtoasters at 2x: step 29.3 to 6.7 ms, 22.3 to 28.5 fps; at 1x: step
  15.9 to 3.7 ms. Fireworkx draws its own squares and did not change.
- `image_data_to_pixmap` accepts a NULL width, height or mask pointer (XMatrix
  passes no mask, and a NULL mask used to crash it on start); with no mask
  pointer no mask is made.
- `XClearWindow` clears to the colour `XSetWindowBackground` last set
  (default 0), and `xshim_release_pixmaps` resets it when a hack stops: the
  display outlives the hack, and Hexadrop's colour once turned Pyro's clear
  into a solid fill. No key events ever arrive, so `XLookupString` finds no
  characters, and an Xt timer (`X11/Intrinsic.h`) is never made.
- The shim still draws nothing into a depth-1 pixmap and draws every GC as
  `GXcopy`; it only remembers the function in `gc->function` now (GXcopy, GXor,
  GXxor). Halo and Moire2 handle both inside their own wrappers
  (`halo_planes.h`, `moire2_planes.h`).
- `screenhack.h`'s `frand` has a `1.0` inside its macro body, so the float
  literal pass cannot reach it and a single-precision wrapper still divides in
  double (software on the S3; `nm` shows `__divdf3`). `hacks/single_frand.h`
  redefines it in float; it is opt-in, because the older wrappers' frame hashes
  are pinned with the original.
- Added for the second batch, each test-first: 16-bit ZPixmap `XImage`s
  (canvas-order pixels, like every other value the shim hands out: `XAllocColor`

  fill-style and stipple constants (accepted, ignored: fills are solid and
  even-odd); and `XSetFunction` and `jwxyz_XSetAlphaAllowed` (no-ops).

  `random()`, so `ya_rand_init` seeds it); `make_color_ramp` (the short way
  round the hue wheel, there and back when `closed_p`; ours, not
  xscreensaver's); `visual_depth` (always 16); `xshm.h` with

  zeroed 16-bit `XImage` and `XPutImage` (`x11shim/xshm.c`); the arrow and page

  `new_string`: an edit that ends at a space in `platformio.ini`'s
  `build_src_filter` glued two entries together (it still built, which hid it).

  transparency (Qix, Goop) falls back to opaque layers and prints "couldn't
  allocate any color planes" on the host.

  been stale since commit 272ad6a: an `XImage` holds canvas-order pixels. A
  hack that builds its own 16-bit image must `px_swap` its pixels first.

  window (onto itself, rows moved with `memmove` in the order that reads each
  first, or into a pixmap); `XSetGraphicsExposures`; `make_color_loop` (ours);
  `grabclient.h` with `load_image_async_simple`, which finishes at once, with
  the grab image painted if one is set (below); `thread_util.h`, a pool that
  runs each thread in turn on the caller, as upstream does without pthreads;
  `visual_pixmap_depth`; `XCharStruct`; and `image_data_to_ximage` (RGBA
  bytes, bottom row first). `screenhack.h` now includes `visual.h` and
  `grabclient.h`, as upstream's does.

  `#ifdef` in the registry, the expected list and `kBaseline`.

  window background, clipped; a width or height of 0 runs to the window's
  edge; Worm), `XMaxRequestSize` (65535, so Lisa batches about 32,000 points a
  call) and the `LineOnOffDash` and `LineDoubleDash` constants (accepted;
  lines still draw solid; Penrose uses them only in its monochrome path). The
  scorer's gap list was wrong for Triangle (`free_colors` and
  `make_smooth_colormap` exist; its xlockmore include chain just does not
  reach `colors.h`, so `hacks/triangle_colors.c` includes `screenhack.h`
  first) and XRaySwarm (`initTime` is the hack's own, behind
  `HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY`, which upstream takes from `config.h`:
  `hacks/xrayswarm_time.c` defines it). Putting `colors.h` in the shim's
  `screenhackI.h` would have fixed Triangle for all but changes what every
  xlockmore hack sees, so it is Rod's call.

  is set where the GC's foreground is odd and cleared where it is even, and the
  clip mask and the GC's function are ignored. The polygon is even-odd, a pixel
  being in when its centre is, in float. Other primitives still draw nothing on
  a bitmap. Halo, Moire2 and Goop keep their own planes or layers and did not
  move.

  picture to paint over its target the next time a load starts: scaled to cover
  and cropped evenly at the sides (a 4:3 screenshot on the square screen loses
  its left and right edges), mask ignored, finishing at once as before. `main.cpp`
  sets it from the header `firmware/grab_image.py` writes into the build
  directory: `firmware/assets/grab-image.png` (Rod's choice: the Windows 95
  screenshot from guidebookgallery.org, committed at his say-so, with a
  notices section), or `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=<file>`, and `XS_GRAB_IMAGE=none` builds
  without. It is stored at up to 466 pixels (a 466 by 350 blob was 340
  KB of flash, 48 KB since it was deflated in #102: the build had gone from
  2.39 MB to 2.74 MB, 87.0% of the app partition). The host tests set their
  own picture, so a pin never depends on the local file; `dump` sets it when
  the header exists. DecayScreen is unpinned for that reason
  (`test_decayscreen_melts_the_grab_image`). Boxfit's `grab` mode, off by
  default, would get the picture too.
- `make_smooth_colormap` follows upstream's behaviour (written from scratch, not
  copied): two to five random points in hue, saturation and value, repicked if
  adjacent ones are close or the average is too grey or dark, joined in a closed
  path with colours spaced by edge length. The first version always spanned the
  hue wheel at high saturation and value, so Triangle and 23 other pinned hacks
  were a bright rainbow.
- The Xft stand-in (`xft.h`, `xft.c`, `xft_font.h`; ours) draws 8-bit coverage
  glyphs, blended over the canvas pixel by pixel (the canvas is byte-swapped
  565, so each pixel is swapped, weighed in 8-bit channels and packed again),
  clipped in 64 bits and marked dirty once a glyph. It ignores the GC's clip
  mask, as Xft does. The glyph data is baked from `assets/fonts/` at 12, 16,
  20 and 24 pixels (`font_atlas.py`): the tables cost about 57 KB of flash
  (87.0% of the app partition became 88.8% with XJack), and a size is picked
  by the number at the end of a font name. `screenhack.h` does not include
  `xft.h`: a hack gets it through a wrapper (`hacks/xjack_xft.c`). With no
  font installed a hack gets a blank one (advance, no ink), because XJack
  `abort()`s on none and `test_pyro` and `test_push_present` run every hack.
- The runner never sends a hack a reshape, and `XClearWindow` clears to
  black unless the hack calls `XSetWindowBackground`, where xscreensaver's
  `screenhack.c` sets the window background from the `background` resource and
  sends a reshape after init. A hack that depends on either needs a wrapper
  (XJack's `xjack_init_on_paper`); doing it in the runner would change what
  every hack sees, so it is Rod's call. Any other registered hack with a
  light `background` that calls `XClearWindow` may have the same fault.
- The shim's `screenhack.h` does not include `screenhackI.h` (upstream's
  does), so plain hacks and xlockmore hacks see different headers. Put a
  macro upstream defines in `screenhackI.h` for every hack into a small
  header both include, as `nls.h` (`_()` and `gettext`) is.

201	    pushes synchronously.

  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (140) must cover the text block plus its outline: the badge
  is two lines, and `stampText` drops any line that would not fit. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38
  (`OLED_TE`), M5GFX programs it (`0x35`, `0x44` at line 466) and nothing waits
  for it. It pulses every 16.82 ms for 1.1 ms. A full push is 20.6 ms copying
  into M5GFX's framebuffer plus 11.7 ms flushing to the panel (split by an
  outer `startWrite()` around the `pushImage`; the flush happens at the
  `endWrite`). `HackEntry::sync_to_refresh` (`XLOCKMORE_HACK_SYNCED`) starts
  the push `kTeSyncOffsetUs` after TE rises (`runner/te_sync.h`). Only
  Unknown Pleasures asks, because it costs up to a refresh of latency a frame.
- The offset (7.4 ms) is the middle of the clean window, found by a sweep:
  eight offsets across one refresh, 3 s each, the step number stamped on the
  screen, filmed at 120 fps. 3.2 to 9.5 ms had no vanished line in 39 updates;
  1.1 and 15.8 ms did, with the seam at film row 495 and film row 268: about 107
  film rows per millisecond (the camera frame is taller than the panel; the
  466-row panel scans about 28 rows per millisecond), so the bad window is only
  about 5 ms wide. It is valid for a full-frame push (the 20.6 ms copy). A push
  of another size moves the flush and the sweep would have to be repeated: the
  QR overlay's 328-row push is one, so a seam may show while the code is up.
  `-DTE_DIAG` logs the TE period and where pushes start.
- `te_sync.c` trusts few edges. Once it knows the period it accepts a rising
  edge only within period/16 of a whole number of periods since the last, so a
  missed edge or a stray pulse cannot move the lock; four misfits in a row drop
  the lock and relearn it. An edge further ahead than one period is stale (the
  32-bit microsecond counter can pass half its range with the line dead), and
  waiting stops 100 ms after the last edge. The ISR is placed in IRAM, but
  Arduino's pin dispatcher and `gpio_get_level` are in flash; that is safe only
  because `CONFIG_ARDUINO_ISR_IRAM` is unset. The run log's `sync=` is the wait
  for the edge and is left out of `push=`: compare `push=` across hacks, and add
  `sync=` to get the frame's latency.
- Reading a film of the display: iPhone slo-mo files store their first and
  last seconds at normal speed, so the label changes every ~100 frames there
  and every 360 in the 120 fps middle. Stabilise against the scenery (four
  corner patches; a mask edge around the display pins phase correlation at
  zero), level the rows, and count a vanish only when a line is missing across
  at least three 24 px windows on one row and not in a settled frame of the
  same update. A detector that finds nothing must also find the event you know
  is there: mine reported zero until a known vanish was used as a control, and
  reported many false events on steep line stretches until settled frames were.
- Every push also dims the screen: the dimmest band falls to 0.86 of its
  settled brightness for about 25 ms (three camera frames at 120 fps), at 5 Hz,
  with or without TE sync (0.860 synced, 0.870 unsynced). It is probably the
  "whole screen redraws" flicker. Its cause is not known. Rod sees no dimming
  with the sparser build (20 rows of 50 points, a step of about 91 ms against
  165), so it may track how much is lit or how long the copy runs; not yet
  filmed (issue #68).
- A hack's returned delay is waited after the push, and only the push counts
  against it, so its own step adds to the frame time: to hold a rate, return
  the target minus the step (`ad_flyingtoasters.c`: 19.5 fps became 28.9).
- PSRAM cost model (`diag/psram_bench.h`, `-DPSRAM_BENCH`): the data cache is
  32 KB, 8-way, 32-byte lines over 80 MHz octal PSRAM, and every miss costs
  about 0.92 us whatever the write size (sequential about 35 MB/s). Firmware
  switches to 64-byte lines (4-way) when a hack starts (`dcache.h`, through
  ROM calls the SDK header says an application should not make): sequential
  passes get about 28% faster and the full-frame push drops from 29 to
  24.8 ms, but a lone short write costs 1.3 us a miss. Pinned A/B, two
  rounds each: Deluxe, Interference, Kumppa, Abstractile +9%, HexTrail +17%,
  Marbling +7%, WhirlWindWarp +6%, Qix and Hexadrop +4%, Gears +3%; Lisa,
  Substrate, XRaySwarm, Pyro, RotZoomer flat. A `sync_to_refresh` hack
  keeps 32 bytes (Unknown Pleasures' offset was swept against the old copy
  time) and so does a hack with `dcache_line32` set in its `HackEntry`
  (Discrete: -5% fps, step 67.9 to 72.8 ms, many short spans). The other core
  is parked in IRAM with interrupts off while the cache is reconfigured
  (`dcache_with_other_core_parked`, over `esp_ipc_call`), as the SDK does for
  flash writes: `noInterrupts()` stops only the calling core.
  `-DDCACHE_LINE32` turns it off for every hack. Compare builds only
  pinned: a free-running lap changes random parameters per visit and showed
  false regressions of 3x on five hacks. A ROM prefetch setting (trigger 1,
  size 0) changed nothing; other settings are untried.
- A hack with `repaints_all` (`hack_entry.h`) draws its next frame while core 0
  pushes the last (`runner/push_overlap.[ch]`, issue #54): two canvases swap
  each frame, the worker pushes the finished one, and the loop credits that
  push's measured duration against the hack's delay. Pinned A/B on the board,
  plain to overlapped: Deluxe 14.0 to 19.0 fps, Compass 18.8 to 29.1, FuzzyFlakes
  18.4 to 28.9, Moire2 16.5 to 26.4, Scooter 22.1 to 28.4; eighteen hacks are
  flagged, five of them GL (grep `repaints_all`, and
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_REPAINTS_ALL`). The step slows by about 5 ms (both cores
  share the PSRAM cache), so the frame is roughly the step, not the longer of
  the two. Rules:
  - Flag a hack only if it never reads the canvas it starts from. The noise
    test and the real-swap test in `test_push_overlap` run every flagged hack
    for 300 frames; 40 frames missed Halo, which the 300-frame run caught. GL
    hacks pass since #118 (see `gl.md`); GraphStat's swap run still fails.
  - Only a gain of 5% or more on a pinned A/B earns the flag. Deco and CCurve
    are paced by their own delays and gained 0 and 2.6%.
  - A hack whose `HackEntry` comes from `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` in the
    byte-identical copy (Truchet, +25%) needs a wrapper to be flagged.
  - Any overlay (name, badge, QR, fps, battery) makes the push synchronous
    while it shows, so the fps overlay reads the plain rate. Read `fps=` in
    the serial log for the overlapped one.
  - Three bugs the spike hit: a redraw from the wait loop must not dispatch a
    second push (it blocked 25 ms), the overlay text canvas wraps one buffer
    and must follow `canvas.px`, and the newest-frame pointer must be dropped
    when a hack starts or Forest's first frame swapped the old picture back.
  - `-DPUSH_NO_OVERLAP` turns it off for every hack (the A side of `ab_flash`).
    The spare canvas is 434 KB of PSRAM; if it will not allocate the firmware
    pushes synchronously.

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere
  in the text of `g_hacks[]`, `#ifdef` or not, and then refuses one that
  `failed_ports.txt` also lists. A probe-only entry (Hypnowheel's
  `HYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`) goes through a macro defined above the array.
- `speed_backtest.py` probes a dropped (shelved) hack standalone. A GL one
  (its source has `USE_GL`: Hypnowheel) is built with the GL layer through
  `gl_budget.measure`, which also converts the `images/gen/<n>_png.h` textures
  it includes. One that still cannot be built (BlockTube needs `glFogi`, which
  the GL layer lacks) is left out with a `note:` on stderr, so read the run's
  output for notes. The scorer also lists calls inside code that is never
  compiled (`XCreateBitmapFromData` in Cynosure's `DO_STIPPLE` block) as gaps.
- `score_hacks.py` skips the names in `OWN_HACKS` (our own hacks with no
  xscreensaver source, now `ad_flyingtoasters`) and still reports any other
  registry name it cannot scan as a typo. `speed_backtest.py` runs on the host
  only the registered hacks that have a device-measured row, so a `dump` build
  without the After Dark disk (which lacks the toasters) still works.
- `probe_hacks.MEASURED_ROW` takes only a number range in the fps cell: a
  row like `| HexTrail | 10.8-50.6, mean 15.3 |` is skipped, so the assessment
  shows `-` for its step and the backtest leaves it out. Put the mean in the
  prose.
- A call to an undeclared shim function also shows up as a gap named
  `error: incompatible integer to pointer conversion ...` (the implicit `int`
  return). It is noise beside the real gap (Barcode's `utf8_to_latin1`), but it
  counts towards the band.

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.17 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only
  appears when there are any). Failures are recorded in
  `tools/failed_ports.txt`.

## Effort ratings

| Rating | Meaning | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | 2D, and the unmodified source compiles against the shim | 4 |
| M | 2D, 1-4 shim gaps, no pixmaps or pixel read-back | 1 |
| L | 2D, 5+ shim gaps, or uses pixmaps or pixel read-back | 40 |
| XL | GL: runs on the TinyGL layer, each hack needs its own GL calls and helpers checked (see below) | 130 |
| Ported | Already running on the device, so no rating | 108 |

# Porting assessment

Rough effort to port each xscreensaver hack to the StopWatch X11 shim,
generated from xscreensaver 6.17 by `tools/score_hacks.py`. Regenerate
it with `uv run tools/score_hacks.py`.

## How to read this

- **283 hacks** were scanned: every `hacks/*.c` and `hacks/glx/*.c`
  that registers itself with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE`. Another 125
  files (3D models, helper libraries, command-line tools) are excluded and
  listed at the end.
- The scan is static and heuristic. For each 2D hack it counts the Xlib
  calls in the source that the shim does not declare, and it also
  syntax-checks the unmodified source against the shim's headers
  (`cc -fsyntax-only`). Anything the compiler cannot find is a **shim
  gap**: a missing header, type, struct field, constant or function.
  That second check catches helpers hacks reach through `utils/` that a
  count of Xlib calls cannot see. The effort rating does not run anything,
  so treat it as a prioritisation aid, not an estimate. It also says nothing
  about speed: see "Speed" below.
- The **All hacks** table lists the work still to do first, from least to
  most effort (S, M, L, XL) and then by name, and the ported hacks last.
  Its **Ported** column shows ✅ for a hack in the
  firmware's registry (`hacks/registry.c`) and ❌ for one that was
  attempted and abandoned (see "Failed ports" after the table, which only

# Working in a git worktree

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- In a git worktree the ignored `vendor/`, `.venv/` and `.platformio/` are
  missing. Symlink them from the main checkout. `.gitignore`'s trailing slashes
  don't match symlinks, so they would show as untracked, but the shared
  `.git/info/exclude` already lists the three names. That file is shared by
  every worktree: ask Rod before adding to it.
  The harness refuses `source tools/env.sh` and a computed `PATH` there: run
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<worktree>/.platformio ../.venv/bin/pio ...` instead,
  and keep commands plain (no scripts, loops, `$VAR` in a command or `&&`
  chains with a computed path). A worktree an agent works in (`isolation:
  "worktree"`) starts from `origin/main`, not from your branch, and has no
  vendor or toolchain until you link them.
  It also refuses heredocs, `git -C` and `cd` into another worktree: use the
  Edit and Write tools. It refuses `git ... | tar` and `cd <dir> && git ...`
  too: use `git archive -o f.tar <sha>` then `tar -x -f f.tar -C <dir>`, and run
  git from the worktree root. A background shell starts there as well, so use
  `pio test -d <abs>/firmware` with absolute paths. Parallel calls can race
  (a `uv run` in the root disturbed `.venv` while `pio` ran:
  "../.venv/bin/pio: no such file"), so run
  `uv` and `pio` one at a time. To fast-forward `main` or remove the worktree,
  leave it first with `ExitWorktree keep`. If no checkout has `main` out,
  `git fetch origin main:main` fast-forwards it from anywhere.
  Before `ExitWorktree remove` on a merged branch, check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main`; the tool's "discarded N
  commits" count ignores merges. `.platformio`, `.venv` and `vendor` there are
  symlinks, so removal leaves the real ones alone. After a merge,
  `ExitWorktree keep` names a branch (`worktree-<name>`) that may not exist:
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` and delete the
  real branch, as separate commands, because a failed `&&` link skips the rest
  silently. Check `git worktree list` afterwards. In a session resumed from a
  summary, `ExitWorktree` is a no-op ("no active EnterWorktree session"):
  remove the worktree with `git worktree remove --force <path>` from the main
  checkout instead. To delete the merged branch
  you are standing on, `git switch --detach origin/main` in the worktree first.
  The shell's directory resets after each command and after `ExitWorktree`, so
  use absolute paths (`../.venv/bin/pio` failed from the wrong place and the run
  looked like a test failure). A loop over several mutations is refused as a
  command: write it as a script in the scratchpad that edits the file, runs
  `pio test` through `subprocess` and restores the file in `finally`, then run
  it with `python3 -I`.
  Stopping such a script (TaskStop) kills it before `finally` runs: check
  `git diff` afterwards and restore the file by hand.
  Also refused: a heredoc (use the Write tool for a scratchpad script), `$(...)`
  inside a git command, and the quoted `PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS` above combined
  with a redirect or `NO_COLOR=1`. Flashing worked as
  `PLATFORMIO_CORE_DIR=<wt>/.platformio PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="..."
  .venv/bin/pio run -d firmware -e stopwatch -t upload` with no redirect: the
  540 KB of output lands in a tool-results file, so grep that for "Hash of data
  verified". Edit and Write refuse the main checkout's path while you are in a
  worktree. `pio test -f test_x` runs the whole suite (`test_hacks` takes 3
  minutes, the full native run 7), and a failing summary reads "2 failed, 101
  succeeded": match `[FAILED]` or the return code, not "succeeded".
- `uv run ty check` (the pre-commit `ty` hook) fails in a worktree with
  "Failed to spawn: ty": the shared `.venv` has no `ty`. Run
  `uvx ty check --python .venv` instead (it passes on a clean tree), then
  commit with `SKIP=ty git commit ...`, and say in the PR that the hook was
  skipped. `ruff-format` rewrites a file and aborts the commit when a line is
  too long: restage the file and commit again.
- Also refused in a worktree session: a shell variable used as a program's
  argument (`S=...; prog $S/x`), a `for` loop that runs `uv` or `pio`, and
  `entire trail finding resolve -m "..."` text containing `*` or backticks.
  Spell out absolute paths, run one command per call, and keep `-m` text to
  plain words.
